activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A necessary condition must hold for something to happen but may not be enough: the sun being above the horizon is necessary for direct sunlight, but not sufficient, since something may cast a shadow.
story:
The seminar room smelled of whiteboard marker and rain, and Amy had claimed the seat by the window because the window at least offered weather, while the room offered only the debate already forming between Laeticia and Amanda about early admission.

"If you have the grades, you're in," Laeticia said, tapping her pen against the table in a rhythm that suggested she had decided this long ago and was merely performing the conclusion. "Ninety-five average, done. Why would they say no?"

Amanda folded her arms. "Because they say no to people with ninety-five all the time. My cousin had a ninety-six and got rejected from three places."

"Then she applied wrong. Grades get you in."

Ms. Siddiqui, who had been writing a single word on the board in her narrow capitals, turned around. The word was NECESSARY, and beneath it she had started SUFFICIENT, but she underlined neither, and instead she said, "Don't solve it yet. Take five minutes and write down what would have to be true for Laeticia's claim to work."

Amy wrote nothing at first. She watched rain stutter down the glass and thought about the sun, which was somewhere above the clouds and doing no one any good. Her mother had said something at breakfast, something about how a clear sky wouldn't help the tomato plants if the neighbour's fence still threw shade over the bed all afternoon, and the two thoughts braided together before Amy quite noticed.

She tried it out on her page. Suppose the sun is above the horizon. That had to be true for anything to be in direct sunlight at all; without it, nothing, no matter how you arranged the garden. But the sun being up didn't guarantee the light landed on you. The fence could be in the way. Something could always cast a shadow. So the sun's position was one of those things that had to hold, and still might not be enough. The grades, then, were like the sun: you couldn't get in without them, probably, but having them didn't finish the argument. The rejection letters were the shadows.

The word Ms. Siddiqui had half-written surfaced, and Amy raised her hand before she had fully decided to. "It's the difference between necessary and sufficient," she said, and heard Laeticia's pen stop tapping. "A necessary condition must hold for something to happen, but it may not be enough. So grades could be necessary without being sufficient." She said it quickly, the way you admit something you're not sure you own yet.

Laeticia turned it over visibly, chin propped, eyes narrowed at the board as if the word there had rearranged itself. "So you're saying grades don't matter."

"No," Amy said. "The opposite, sort of. They matter the way the sun matters. Take them away and nothing happens. But they can't be the whole story, because your claim needs something else to be true too. It needs the admissions office to have no better candidates, or no quota, or no bad mood that morning." She could feel the edges of what she didn't know. "I can't actually prove grades are necessary. Maybe someone gets in without them. That part I'd have to check."

"You're saying nobody can promise you anything," Amanda said, not triumphantly, which surprised Amy, who had expected triumph.

"I'm saying a promise has parts. If someone promises you'll get in, they're quietly promising a whole chain of things, and the grades only underwrite the first link." Amy had found the word in a book about bridge engineering the previous summer and had been waiting months to use it somewhere it actually fit.

Ms. Siddiqui asked the class what other claims might have this shape, and the room loosened into speculation. Someone proposed that water was necessary for a river, and a boy in the back row objected that water wasn't sufficient for a river either, that a ditch full of rainwater was not a river, and the argument drifted toward what made a river a river until the boy, reaching, said something about the plants along the banks, the riparian growth, being part of what people meant. Laeticia said that calling a drainage ditch a river would be a travesty of a river, and the boy said a small river wasn't a travesty of a big one, and Amy wrote both sentences down because she couldn't yet say which was right.

When the bell rang, Laeticia lingered, gathering her things slower than usual. "So if I get the grades," she said, backpack half on, "and I don't get in, it's not because the grades failed."

"It's not because they were nothing," Amy said. "It's because they were the sun and the fence was still there."

Laeticia looked at her a second longer than the conversation seemed to require, then said, "I hate that," and almost smiled, and pushed the door open into the rain.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface.
story:
Riley had one weekend to finish the backdrop for June's short film, and the plywood street he'd painted in the backyard looked like something a neophyte would tape to the wall of a kindergarten. Buildings stood side by side like playing cards, flat and shameless, refusing to be a street at all. June had already sent two texts asking if it would be ready. The third text, that morning, had said only, "We shoot Sunday." He knelt on the old drop cloth behind the garage, brush in hand, and considered that painting this thing properly might be the only way to expiate the mess he'd made of last week, when he'd told the whole group their film was basically a home movie with delusions.

Karen came through the side gate carrying two cans of lemonade, which she set down on the grass without asking whether he wanted them. She looked at the plywood for a long time, the way she looked at everything, as though it had disappointed her personally.

"It's flat," she said.

"Thank you, Karen."

"No, I mean it's really flat. Like the buildings are all standing in a police lineup. Facing forward. Nobody's turned."

He wiped his hands on his jeans and tried to see it the way she did. She was right, and he hated that she was right, and he said so, which surprised them both. She sat down on the antiquated milk crate his grandfather had left by the fence and turned the plywood toward the afternoon light. Then she took the pencil from behind her ear, the one she always carried for reasons nobody had ever established, and drew a single dot in the middle of the street, low, near the bottom edge.

"What's that?"

"Vanishing point," she said. "From art history. Mr. Mokoena made us copy it off the board."

Riley stared at the dot. Something Mr. Mokoena had said came back to him, something about Florence, around 1420, when a man named Brunelleschi had demonstrated linear perspective to the public, a way of drawing lines that met at a point like this one so that depth appeared on a flat surface. Riley had written it down at the time only because it was going to be on the test. Now he stood up, took the pencil from Karen, and laid a ruler from the dot to the edge of the board, then another line, then another. The edges of his buildings, extended backward, would all run toward that single point. His windows, his curbstones, the lintels over the doors. Every line converging.

"Get me the blue tape," he said.

They worked until the light went orange. He repainted the faces of the buildings, angling their tops inward, sliding the windows into slanted parallelograms that all leaned toward the dot. Karen held the ruler and told him when a line wandered. At some point his mother called from the kitchen window that she was ordering pizza, and neither of them answered, and she didn't repeat it. When he finally stepped back past the drop cloth, past the milk crate, all the way to the fence, the street opened. It lay there in the grass like a canyon, the buildings folding away from him, the far end of the painted road narrowing toward a bright impossible distance. His chest did something he didn't have a word for.

June arrived Sunday morning with her camera and her older cousin and a borrowed reflector, walked into the backyard, and stopped so abruptly the cousin bumped into her. She looked at the backdrop, then at Riley, then at the backdrop again.

"You did this," she said. It wasn't entirely a question. He shrugged, and she kept staring, and he understood that she was recalculating him, revising whatever version of him she'd been carrying since his home movie comment. He let her. Some of it he'd earned.

They carried the plywood to the front of the house and set it against the porch rail for the shot, and it was there, framing it through the camera, that June found the twist. Behind the painted street, visible exactly at the vanishing point through the gap between two painted buildings, stood the real alley that ran beside Riley's house, its fence receding to its own far point. Painted depth and true depth met at the dot as if they'd planned it for years. June looked through the lens for a long moment without speaking.

"Leave it exactly there," she said. "Nobody touches anything."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Under US law, an artwork is protected by copyright automatically the moment it is created in a fixed form; registration is voluntary, though needed before suing over a US work.
story:
The porch at her grandmother's house had become Isabella's studio by default, since the kitchen table was reserved for canning and the attic was full of her grandfather's taxidermied pheasants, which she refused to work beneath. She had taped ten sheets of newsprint along the railing, each one a study for the portfolio due in three weeks, and each one, she had to admit, about something different. A drowning bicycle. Her grandmother's hands. A gas station at dusk. Mr. Villanueva had said a portfolio needed a single theme, ten pieces that argued one position, plus an artist's statement of three hundred words explaining what that position was.

"I don't have a position," she said to Zayan, who had biked over ostensibly to help but was currently being entralled by the pheasants through the attic window. "I have ten things I can draw."

"Those are different," Zayan said. "A position is like a thesis statement. Mrs. Okafor made us write one for every essay junior year."

"An artist's statement isn't an essay."

"It's three hundred words. It's an essay with better lighting."

Natasha arrived the next afternoon carrying her laptop and a grievance. Someone at the summer program had told her that if she posted her portfolio pieces online, anyone could take them, and she'd spent the morning in a state that was half grief, half litigation fantasy. Isabella, who needed any excuse to stop deciding on a theme, sat with her at the porch table and typed while Natasha talked.

"Okay," Isabella said, scrolling. "So this is the opposite of what that guy said. Under US law, an artwork is protected by copyright automatically, the moment it's created in a fixed form. Like, you drew it, it exists, it's yours."

"So I don't have to mail myself a copy? Someone told me to mail myself a copy."

"That's the poor man's copyright thing, which sounds fake and apparently is. There's more here. It says registration is voluntary." Isabella read further, then turned the screen. "But you'd need it before suing over a US work."

Natasha looked at the page for a long moment. "So it's mine, but I can't do anything about it unless I register."

"Voluntary but required," Isabella said. "Which is a very legal way of saying yes and no at the same time."

The afternoon had that thick late-August somnolence where the cicadas seemed to be running at half speed, and the two of them sat with the fact. Natasha registered her twelve pieces that evening, at her mother's kitchen table, and texted Isabella a screenshot with no caption. Isabella, meanwhile, kept thinking about the word "fixed." Created in a fixed form. Her ten sheets of newsprint were fixed. They existed, therefore they were hers, and yet they didn't argue anything. She had automatic protection and no position, which felt like a metaphor she couldn't quite close.

She called Zayan the next morning. "I think my theme is custody," she said. "Like, what's yours automatically, and what you have to claim on purpose. The bicycle drowned and it's still somebody's. My grandmother's hands and everything they've held. The gas station, which nobody owns after ten p.m."

"Copyright as a theme," Zayan said. "That's either brilliant or gratuitous."

"It's not about copyright. Copyright is just the proof of concept." She was already sketching on the back of a gas station receipt. "The statement practically writes itself. What belongs to you the moment you fix it, and what stays contested."

She spent the weekend replacing four of the weakest sheets. Her grandmother brought out iced tea and lingered over the new drawings, one hand on the porch rail, and Isabella drew the hand from memory afterward, quickly, before the somnolence of the afternoon could soften it into something prettier. Mr. Villanueva reviewed the portfolio on Monday and wrote "coherent, finally" in the margin, which from him was extravagant.

On the last night before submission, she and Natasha sat on the porch uploading images. Isabella hovered over the post button, then looked at her friend. "You registered before you posted," she said.

"Twelve pieces, certificate and everything."

Isabella clicked post. The ten images loaded one after another, hers the moment she'd fixed them, whatever that turned out to be worth. "Three hundred words," she said, opening the statement, and began to type: "What is mine the instant I make it."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In common-law countries such as the US, UK and Canada, a contract generally needs an offer, an acceptance and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange.
story:
The phone store smelled of floor polish and warm plastic, and every surface gleamed with the specific brightness of things that had not yet been owned. Adam stood at the counter with two hundred and forty dollars folded in his pocket, listening to the cashier explain that the plan he wanted required a two-year agreement, that the terms and conditions ran to eleven pages, and that by signing he would accept liability for any damage to the device beyond the manufacturer's warranty. He nodded along as though he understood all of it, which he did not, though he understood enough to know the signature line at the bottom was the point toward which everything else flowed.

The problem was simpler than the paperwork. He was seventeen. The cashier had already slid a form toward him marked CONSENT OF PARENT OR GUARDIAN, and Adam had said, with more confidence than he felt, that his mother was on her way. She was not. She was at work until six, and she had told him last week that if he wanted a phone he should pay for it himself, which he had, almost, which was the second problem.

The money was the tutoring money. In September, Yoan had sat across from him in the library and said, "I'll pay you twenty bucks a session if you get me through pre-calc." Adam had laughed and said sure, and for three months they had met on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and Yoan's grades had climbed from a D to a B-minus, and the cash had come in dribbles, a ten here, a twenty there, until the tally on Adam's phone said Yoan owed him ninety dollars. When Adam had finally texted about it, Yoan had replied that he'd thought it was more of a friend thing, that they'd never shaken on it, that Adam was making it weird.

"You can't impugn my honor over some vague thing I said in the library," Yoan had said at lunch, in that half-joking voice he used when he wanted a complaint to sound like a compliment to himself. Adam hadn't known what to say then. He still didn't. What he knew was that he had given up forty-odd evenings, and Yoan had taken what those evenings offered, and the distance between those two facts was exactly ninety dollars wide.

Behind the counter, Mr. Eze, the manager, was ringing up a woman's trade-in. Adam had been in the store twenty minutes and had watched him work the whole time: patient, unhurried, initialing the boxes on the contract where the initials were required, explaining deductibles in a voice that made eleven pages of terms sound almost reasonable. There was something steadying about the man, and when the woman left, Adam found himself asking, without quite planning to, whether a promise counted as a contract if nobody had signed anything.

Mr. Eze considered him over the rims of his glasses. "Depends. What'd you give up for it?"

Adam told him about the evenings in the library, and the twenty dollars a session, and Yoan's friend thing.

"Then it's not just talk," Mr. Eze said, and turned to his screen. He was not a man who lectured, Adam realized; he was a man who had spent years watching people discover what they had already agreed to. "My daughter tried that on me once over dishes. Didn't work either."

Adam was still turning this over when the door chimed and Yoan came in with Steven, both of them ostensibly shopping, actually lingering, the way they did everywhere, treating the mall as a kind of public living room. Yoan spotted Adam at the counter and drifted over with the wariness of someone who suspects a trap. Steven followed, grinning, and picked up a display phone and began photographing himself with it in slow, ceremonial poses.

"What are you doing here with all the contracts," Yoan said. "Getting your whole life away."

"Getting a phone," Adam said. "The money I'm paying with it with."

That was when Yoan went quiet in a way Adam had rarely seen. Steven lowered the display phone. Mr. Eze, who had been watching with mild professional interest, said nothing at all.

From where Mr. Eze stood, the two boys by the counter looked like a negotiation about to happen whether they wanted one or not. He had seen this shape a hundred times in the store: the pause before acceptance, the small tectonic shift in a person's posture when they understood that a decision had already been made somewhere inside them and was now merely catching up. The younger one, the one with the folded cash, stood very straight. The other one's shoulders had dropped half an inch.

"I looked it up," Adam said. "After lunch. A contract needs an offer, an acceptance, and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange. You offered twenty a session. I accepted. I gave the sessions. You gave some of the money. That's it. That's the whole thing. It doesn't need a signature."

"It needs my ninety dollars, apparently," Yoan said, but he said it without heat, and Steven, unhelpfully, said, "Dude got you. That's like law."

Yoan pulled out his wallet at the counter like a man surrendering something larger than cash. He counted out sixty dollars, said his checking account had the rest but the card was at home, and offered the sixty as what he called a first installment, using the word with exaggerated formality, as though the store were teaching him its vocabulary by proximity. Adam took it. He did not say it was fine, because it was not fine, exactly, and he did not say they were done, because he was not sure they were, and the difference between those two uncertainties felt like something he would understand better in a year.

With three hundred dollars in his pocket, the plan was suddenly affordable, and the consent form was suddenly the only obstacle, and Adam stood there looking at the line where his mother's signature belonged. He thought about calling her at work, about the terms she would want explained, about whether she would say the two-year agreement was a lesson in commitment or just a company's way of holding him. Mr. Eze waited, pen resting on the counter between them like an offer nobody had accepted yet.

"Your mom's number," Mr. Eze said. "We can go over the terms with her on the phone, and she can come sign tonight. Or you can think about it."

Adam picked up the pen, then set it back down, and dialed.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie, first staged in Chicago in 1944, a memory play: it is narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family.
story:
I don't care what Alexi thinks, so it didn't matter that she laughed when I said I was writing about the night my father left. It didn't matter at all. Ms. Tesfaye had told us on the first day of drama camp to pick a real moment, one we could hold in our hands, and I had that one, even if the details kept sliding around when I reached for them. Was it raining? I said it was raining in my first draft. In my second draft I made it snow, because snow is better staging, and by then I honestly couldn't have told you which was true.

The rehearsal hall at the camp was an old gym with a stage at one end and folding chairs stacked against the wall. On Tuesday we did an exercise where we walked the space while Ms. Tesfaye called out directions, and afterwards we sat on the floor in a circle with our notebooks. Joshua read his opening aloud, something about a bus station, and Alexi read hers, which was about her grandmother's kitchen and was, I'll admit, good. Then everyone looked at me and I said I hadn't finished, which was true, mostly. I had six pages. I just didn't want to hear them yet.

"You could use a narrator," Alexi said after, in the hallway by the water fountain. "Like Tennessee Williams. He called The Glass Menagerie a memory play. It first played in Chicago, in 1944, and it's narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family." She said it fast, the way she recited things when she wanted you to know she'd done the reading.

"Memory play," I repeated. I liked the weight of it. I liked the word "etymology" too, which Ms. Tesfaye had written on the board that morning, tracing "theatre" back through Greek, and I'd sat there feeling that words had trapdoors in them, that you could fall through a word into its past.

I didn't tell Alexi I was going to steal the idea. That night in the dorm I rewrote the whole thing. My play was now narrated by a girl standing at the edge of the stage, stepping out of the scene to tell the audience what it meant, the way Tom does. The narrator said things like "This is how I remember it, which is not how it happened," and I thought that line was brilliant until I realized I had written it because it was literally my situation. I had changed the rain to snow. I had moved the argument from the kitchen to the driveway because the driveway was easier to block with two chairs.

At Friday's run-through I made Joshua play my father and Alexi play my mother, and I stood at the edge of the taped square of light and narrated. "My father left in November," I said. Joshua shifted his weight. Alexi, in her one chair, kept her eyes on the middle distance, which was the right choice, and the whole thing mesmerized me for about four minutes, the way hearing your own voice come back at you from a distance can, until I got to the part where the narrator says the car door slammed twice, and I stopped.

It had slammed once. I was suddenly certain of that. Once, not twice, and I had doubled it because once sounded thin on the page.

"Keep going," Ms. Tesfaye said from the folding chairs.

"I got it wrong," I said.

"Which part?"

"The door. And the snow. And where they were standing." The audience of eleven campers waited. Alexi was still in her chair, still not looking at me, and I understood that she had known, probably since Tuesday, that I'd taken her suggestion without saying so, and that she had given it to me anyway, and that I still wasn't going to thank her right then because some part of me wanted the idea to be mine.

Ms. Tesfaye didn't rescue me. She said, "So what does the narrator say now?" and sat back, and I stood in the square of light for what felt like a long time, hearing the gym fan turn overhead. Then I said the line about the door slamming twice, and I said, "She remembers it twice because once wasn't enough to carry," and Joshua looked up, and Alexi closed her eyes for a second like I'd stepped on her foot.

Afterward, outside, Alexi was waiting by the bike rack with her backpack on one shoulder, cosmopolitan in her sunhat and sunglasses, or at least performing it, which at our age is the same thing. "Chicago, 1944," she said. "You're going to say it in the talkback, right? Give me my citation."

"I'll say it," I said. "And Alexi, was it raining that November, do you remember? You were at my house that weekend."

She pushed her sunglasses up into her hair and looked at me. "Payton," she said, "I've never been to your house."

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The Soviet Union diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea lost a fishing industry that had employed about 40,000 people.
story:
The poster board wouldn't lie flat, and Cole pressed his palm against the corner while Amalia smoothed the tape. They had until Friday to argue their side of the valley water dispute in front of Ms. Flores's geography class, and the county's proposal sat between them on the lab table: divert part of Willow Creek to irrigate eighty acres of new almond orchards upstream. Cole had wanted the easy side. He had asked Ms. Flores for the farmers, and she had looked at him for a long second before saying the county had already assigned the farmers to Johnny's team, and perhaps it would be useful for him to argue against something he wanted to believe.

He believed in the orchards, or he had. His uncle had planted walnuts two counties over, and those trees had kept his uncle's farm solvent through three dry summers, kept the truck payments made, kept his cousins in school shoes. Water in a ditch meant money in a family. That was arithmetic anyone could do.

Amalia spread the county maps across three desks and pinned the creek's path with her finger. "The orchards sit here. The town draws its water here." Between the two points sat eleven miles of river, a swimming hole the summer camp used, and three small farms that had senior water rights, whatever those turned out to be worth in a dry year. "The county says the orchards bring jobs," she said. "Construction, processing, hauling."

"That's what my uncle would say." Cole looked at the map, then at the shelf behind him, where Ms. Flores kept her old atlases, the ones with the cracked spines that nobody was supposed to touch but everybody did. He pulled down the one covering Central Asia, mostly because he was stalling, and because Johnny had spent lunch being bombastic about growth and progress until Cole had wanted to throw a tangerine at him.

The atlas fell open to a page he hadn't expected. A photograph showed a desert, pale and rippled, with the ghost of a harbor in it, rusted hulls sitting upright in sand. Amalia leaned in beside him. "That's the Aral Sea," she read. "Or it was." They followed the captions like a trail. The Soviet Union had diverted the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton. The sea had shrunk and grown saltier. The fishing industry that had employed about 40,000 people was gone.

Cole sat back. He thought of a day years before, the summer he was eleven, when he and his grandfather had gone to the lake where the old man had worked the docks as a young man and found the water so low the boats rested in mud. His grandfather had remonstrated with the marina manager, a polite, useless argument about who had decided to open the upstream gates, and on the drive home he had said nothing at all, only tapped the wheel at the long light by the grain elevator. Cole had thought then that it was just weather.

"It wasn't weather," he said now, to the atlas more than to Amalia. "It was a decision. Somebody upstream got cotton, and forty thousand people downstream got boats in the sand." He was aware that this cut against him, that his uncle's walnuts sat on the wrong side of the ledger he was building, and he wrote it down anyway.

On Friday the room smelled like whiteboard marker and the rain coming through the vents. Johnny opened for the orchards, all confidence and hand gestures, jobs and tax base and the county's future. When Cole stood, he spread the photograph of the ship in the desert. He told the class what the Soviet Union had done to the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, the cotton, the shrinking, saltier sea, the forty thousand fishing jobs gone, and then he said the thing that had taken him until two in the morning to figure out how to say. "I think the orchards might still be worth it. I can't prove they aren't. But somebody should have to say out loud who's downstream, and what they lose, before we count only what we gain."

The twist came during questions. Johnny, flushed, hands shoved in his pockets, said, "My dad's the one leasing the land to the orchard company. I told him your Aral Sea thing at dinner." A pause, the radiator ticking. "He didn't have an answer. He said nobody's counting forty thousand people here, it's just eleven miles of creek. Then he counted them anyway. He's calling the county on Monday to ask what the camp and the small farms are supposed to do."

Ms. Flores wrote something in her binder and did not read it aloud. The bell rang, and the room emptied into the smell of rain, and Cole looked at the photograph one more time before sliding it back into the atlas, the hull beached in all that pale sand, the harbor still faintly holding its shape.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
The envelope had come on Thursday, and by Saturday morning it was still lying on the kitchen table, unopened, with Sienna's mother's reading glasses resting on top of it like a paperweight. It was from Aldergate, the expensive one, the one with the quad she had walked across on a visit in October while a tour guide eulogized the bell tower as if it had recently died. She had applied to six places. Two had said no. One had said yes with a scholarship attached. Aldergate had said only: an envelope thick enough to be either.

Charlene arrived at ten with her laptop bag and half a bagel, because they had promised to compare financial aid letters together, a task Sienna had been postponing with the discipline of someone postponing a dental appointment. "You haven't opened it," Charlene said, setting down the bagel.

"I'm waiting for the right moment."

"It's been two days."

"I'm being strategic." Sienna pulled out the chair across from her, and Charlene sat, opened the laptop, and turned it so they could both see the spreadsheet she had built, color-coded, ruthless. Sienna had spent the spring learning a vocabulary she had never needed before: expected family contribution, net price calculator, work-study. Somewhere in that research she had found a distinction that had rearranged her whole list. "Okay, so you know how I moved Whitmore up and pulled Halloran down?" she said. "Whitmore is need-blind. They decide who gets in without ever looking at whether you can pay. Halloran's need-aware. They look."

Charlene frowned at the screen. "That's legal?"

"Apparently it's common. Most of them are need-aware. Only some decide without it."

"And you found this out after you applied to Halloran."

"After I got in, actually." Which was the part that sat strangely with her. She had been accepted by a college that might have weighed her mother's income on the same scale as her essay. She couldn't decide whether to feel lucky or appraised.

Her mother came through in her scrubs, night shift ending, and set the kettle on. "Did you open it?" she asked, not stopping.

"Almost," Sienna said.

"That's not an answer." The kettle began its low hum. Her mother rested a hand on the back of Charlene's chair, looking at the spreadsheet over her shoulder, and Sienna watched her take in the column marked EFC, the number the federal government had decided their family could contribute, a number that would have been funny if it weren't going to be a mortgage payment. "The Duarte one," her mother said. "That's the full ride."

"Not full. Ninety percent."

"Charlene, talk some sense into her." She went upstairs without waiting for an answer.

Charlene had her own stack of letters in the laptop bag, and Sienna knew, because Charlene had told her in February and then never again, that her first choice was a conservatory in the city, and that her father had said flatly that he wasn't paying for a music degree, and that Charlene had spent three months being very sanguine about the backup school in a way that fooled everyone except, possibly, no one. "What are you going to do?" Sienna asked her now, meaning the conservatory, and Charlene closed the spreadsheet window and opened the aid letter from the backup, which was generous, which was practical, which was everything a person in her position was supposed to want.

"Can we do the envelope first?" Charlene said.

So Sienna picked up the reading glasses, set them aside, and opened it with the butter knife because she couldn't find the letter opener. The letter inside was one page. She read it standing, then sat down and read it again, because the first read had felt like a rumor. Accepted. No mention of money, none at all, only a line directing her to the financial aid portal, which meant the news came in two pieces now, and one of the pieces didn't exist yet, and the deposit deadline was in eleven days.

"Aldergate's need-blind too," Charlene said quietly, scrolling on her phone. "It's on that list you sent me."

It was. Sienna looked at the spreadsheet, at Whitmore in the second row and Aldergate now colored green, and at the Duarte letter in its folder by the fruit bowl, ninety percent, a number that already existed, that she could hold. Her mother came back down in her sleep shirt and stood at the counter with her tea, waiting, and Sienna understood that whatever she said next was going to be heard as a decision even if she didn't mean it as one, and that the truism about doors closing was useless here, because every door was open and she could still only walk through one.

"Can I think about it at lunch?" she said.

"You can think about it out loud," her mother said, and pulled out the third chair.

"Pass me the Duarte letter," Sienna said. "And the laptop. And don't let me be noble about this."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: If two countries give up exactly the same amount of one good to make the other, neither has a comparative advantage, and Ricardo's model predicts no gain from specializing.
story:
The food court at four o'clock was spartan in a way it never was at noon, half the counters dark, the tables wiped and gleaming under the skylights. Robert spread his economics textbook across two chairs and set his binder on the tray ledge beside a half-finished lemonade. Jessy arrived carrying a paper cup of fries she had no intention of finishing and a chemistry review sheet she clearly intended to finish, or at least to hold like a shield.

"You're doing the trade problems already," she said, dropping into the seat across from him. "Mr. Sun only assigned the first ten."

"I did the first ten. They all worked. Portugal makes wine, England makes cloth, both countries end up better off. It's tidy." He turned to problem eleven and flattened the page with his palm. "This one's broken."

Jessy leaned over her fries, chewing, patient in the way she was patient, which was to say she would listen for exactly as long as it took her own worksheet to call her back. Robert read the numbers aloud. Two countries, two goods, output per worker per day. He wrote the ratios in the margin, tongue pressed against his teeth. Country A gives up three units of wheat for every unit of cloth it makes. He flipped his pencil to the eraser end, tapped the page twice, then did the same arithmetic for Country B, and stopped.

"Same," he said. "Three to one. Both of them, exactly three to one." He checked it a second time, multiplying and dividing under his breath, and then a third time in the corner of the page where the paper was clean. "The answer key says trade wouldn't help them. But they're different countries. One of them has to be better at something."

Jessy slid her chemistry sheet aside. On it, in her small upright hand, she had written the word enthalpy three times, once circled, once crossed out, once underlined, as if repetition might make the concept settle. "Better at something," she repeated. "Isn't that the whole point? Like you're better at econ and I'm better at chemistry, so we trade tutoring."

"That's what I thought. But look." He externalized it the only way he knew how, drawing two little grids on a napkin, arrows between them, the way the textbook drew England and Portugal. "In every other problem, the ratios are different. One country gives up two wheat for a cloth, the other gives up four. Then it's obvious who should make what. Here they give up the same amount. Three for one, three for one. It's like they're the same country wearing different hats."

"So what's the answer?"

"The answer says no gain. No gain from specializing. And I think that's the actual answer, not a printing mistake, because the question asks why, and the why is the part I can't write down yet."

Devan appeared then, coming off his shift at the shoe store with his name tag still pinned to his shirt and a bag of pretzel pieces he'd been given for free at closing. He pulled a chair around backward and sat with his arms folded across its backrest. "I could hear you from the fountain," he said. "Something about hats."

Robert slid the napkin toward him. "If two countries give up exactly the same amount of one good to make the other, neither one has the advantage. That's what the ratio means. It's called comparative advantage, and neither of them has it."

Devan studied the napkin as if it were a map of a place he might visit. "So the model just says no?"

"Ricardo's model," Robert said, checking the chapter heading to be sure he had the name right. "It predicts no gain from specializing when it's like this. Which is strange, because everything before this problem made trade look like magic. Like it always pays." He looked at the skylight, where the afternoon light had gone long and orange across the empty tables. "But it doesn't always pay. Sometimes two places are mirrored and there's nothing to gain by splitting up the work."

"Then write that," Jessy said.

"It feels like saying the math ran out. Like I'm admitting I only believe in trade when the numbers are polite."

"But you checked it three times. You checked it more than you've ever checked anything, including your driver's permit test." She pulled her chemistry sheet back toward herself, then stopped, pen hovering. "The enthalpy thing is like this, I think. The formula works until a condition changes, and then you have to know why it stops working, or you'll apply it somewhere it doesn't belong. Maybe that's the answer. Not that trade is bad. Just that this tool has an edge to it."

Robert wrote nothing down for a moment. The pretzel bag rustled. Somewhere behind the dark counters a mop bucket wheeled and squeaked, and the zamboni of the cleaning crew made its slow passes between the rows of chairs.

"There's still something I can't get," he admitted. "Real countries aren't two numbers on a napkin. There has to be more going on than ratios. But the problem only gives me ratios, so the honest answer is the ratio answer." He picked up his pencil, and beneath the two identical fractions, in handwriting smaller and more careful than the rest, he wrote: identical opportunity costs, no comparative advantage, no gain predicted, and then, after a pause, he added a question mark after the word predicted.

Devan reached across and stole a cold fry. "So is that an A or a complaint?"

"That's me saying I believe it as far as it goes," Robert said, and closed the book on the napkin to keep it.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by delaying ovulation, and they are more effective the sooner they are taken after unprotected sex.
story:
Evan had been volunteering at the clinic for six weeks, mostly folding pamphlets and restocking the bowl of condoms by the door, and he had begun to think he was learning a language he would need someday without knowing when. Then Ajay called him on a Saturday night, voice thin and hurried, and said the condom had broken and his girlfriend was frightened and neither of them knew what to do except panic. Evan said, "Stay there. I'm coming over and we're finding a pharmacy that's open."

They walked through the neighbourhood in the dark, past shuttered stores and one bodega whose lights buzzed with a malevolent sort of persistence, while Ajay kept saying he felt like a criminal. "You're not a criminal," Evan said. "You're a person who needs a pill." In his pocket he had the leaflet he'd taken from the clinic, the one he'd read three times while sitting at the front desk with nothing else to do. At the all-night pharmacy the cashier pointed them to the right aisle without any ceremony at all, which surprised Ajay so much he laughed once, sharp and relieved.

The pharmacist, a woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, asked how long ago it had been. Ajay said about five hours. She nodded and said that was good timing, because emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by delaying ovulation, and they're more effective the sooner they're taken after unprotected sex. She said it plainly, the way she might have said take with food, and Evan felt the leaflet in his pocket go from paper to something more like a key. Ajay paid, and on the walk home he held the little box the way you hold a phone you're afraid of dropping.

That was Saturday. On Monday after school, Evan sat in the clinic's waiting room with Mr. Warsame, the health educator who supervised him, going over the binder of scripts Evan was supposed to learn: how to explain consent, how to talk about contraception options, how to tell a nervous teenager that getting tested for infections was routine and quick and nothing to be ashamed of. "Say it back to me," Mr. Warsame said, "in your own words, like you're talking to someone your age, not someone in a textbook." Evan fumbled it the first time. Consent wasn't just the absence of no, he said slowly, it was the presence of yes, given freely, and it could be taken back, and it only counted for what it actually covered. Saying it out loud was different from reading it. He got it wrong twice, then right, and Mr. Warsame said, "Better. Now stop apologizing between sentences."

Evan's father had never explained any of this to him, and Evan understood, in a way he couldn't have put into words a year ago, that the silence was a kind of patrimony, handed down along with the good shoulders and the stubbornness, and that he could refuse his share of it. He was still working out what he believed about all of it. He knew the facts now, the pill and the timing and the clinics, but facts and beliefs sat side by side in him without quite touching, and he was honest enough with himself to admit he didn't know if that gap would ever close. He only knew which silence he wasn't going to pass on.

Which was why, when Landen walked into the waiting room at four-thirty with his hood up and his hands jammed in his pockets, Evan didn't look away. Landen had spent all of eleventh grade calling the clinic a trap, saying they took your information and used it against you, that the whole system was set up to catch people out. Now he stood by the condom bowl, not touching it, staring at a poster about testing. "I'm only here because my brother said they do walk-ins," Landen said. "Don't make it a thing."

"It's not a thing," Evan said. He got the intake clipboard and set it on the counter in front of Landen, and while Landen filled in his name with the careful handwriting of someone vandalizing something, Evan explained what would happen next: a short form, a nurse, a swab or a blood draw depending, results in a few days by text or a call, whichever Landen preferred. "Nobody calls your house," Evan said. "It's your information. You decide who gets it." Landen looked up at him then, and something in his face rearranged itself, a gate unbolting. "Fine," he said. "Fine. But you're sitting in the waiting room the whole time." Evan said he was, and he did, and when Landen came out twenty minutes later with a sticker on his arm and an appointment card he actually put in his wallet instead of his pocket, Evan handed him the same leaflet about testing he'd once read three times behind the front desk. "You can give that to your brother too," he said, and Landen folded it in half, put it in his back pocket, and said, "Ajay says the pharmacist on Fifth is open late."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade.
story:
The grade seven team lost their third game in a row on a Thursday in November, and afterward the coach, a tired man who ran a hardware store, took Elliot aside by the bleachers and said the job was his until Christmas. Elliot was sixteen and had expected to be a player this year, not a bench boss for twelve-year-olds, but the pay was forty dollars a week and his mother had already spent it on his winter boots. He said yes at midcourt with the sound of the ball still echoing off the far wall.

The problem was not hard to see. Every pass the kids threw travelled in a flat, hopeful line at chest height, and every defender in the league had learned to stand in that line with his arms out. Twelve turnovers a game, minimum. Elliot wrote it in his notebook like a diagnosis and then sat for two evenings trying to operationalize it, turning the word weakness into drills, into cones, into something the boys could repeat until their arms remembered. He had three drills ready by Saturday and none of them worked. The kids could pass to a stationary target beautifully. The moment a defender's hand came up, the ball died there.

He was complaining about it on Sunday at Trevor's place, where the game on television was hockey, not basketball. Elliot barely followed hockey. He was halfway through a rant about lazy passes when he stopped, because on the screen a player flicked the puck and it rose, barely, an inch of air under it, sailed flat across the zone, over the outstretched stick of a sprawled defender, and dropped neatly onto a teammate's blade. The commentator barely paused.

"What was that," Elliot said.

"Saucer pass," Trevor said, not looking up from his phone. "My neighbour taught me. Puck lifts just off the ice, flies flat over the guy's stick, lands right on the blade."

The neighbour was Ms. Ivanova, who had lived beside Trevor's family for thirty years and still flooded a rink in her backyard every December. She was watering it when they cut through her yard later, an ascetic figure in the cold, methodical, wrapped in a scarf that had outlasted several governments. Elliot asked her about the pass. She demonstrated twice with a flat rock across the ice, said nothing while he watched, and went back to dragging the hose.

He thought about it the whole walk home. The principle, as far as he could tell, was altitude: the pass chooses a height the defender's stick cannot occupy, then comes down where the receiver actually is. Basketball had no ice and no blade, but it had hands instead of sticks, and hands had limits too. On Monday he drew up a new drill. Two lines, one passer, one receiver, and between them a defender whose only job was to hold his arms straight up and touch nothing. The pass had to arc over the fingertips and arrive soft, catchable, at the chest. He called it the rainbow drill because the kids would remember that.

The first practice was entropy. Balls sailed out of bounds, thumped off shoulders, chased a small guard named Danny into the corner. Farah, who came to every practice because her little brother was on the team and their mother worked evenings, stood under the hoop collecting strays. She wanted her brother at point guard, had said so twice already, wanted the offense flowing through the smallest and smartest kid on the floor, and Elliot had kept him on the wing because the wing was safer. That night she carried the ball back to the rack and said, "He's the only one who can see over the drill you built." Elliot said he'd think about it, and hated the sound of it, and thought about it.

By the third week it worked, mostly. The passes that got through went over the fingertips and landed in the receiver's hands, soft, exactly where the arms ended and the chest began. The turnovers dropped from twelve to five in one game, then four. But the drill cost something too: the arcing pass was slower, and twice a faster team stepped back into the landing spot and stole it anyway, and Danny, moved to point guard at last, threw one full-court saucer that Elliot admired privately for its nerve and then had to bench him for. Some heights still weren't safe. He didn't know yet whether that was a flaw in the drill or in the game itself.

The last practice before the holiday tournament ended with the rainbow drill, the gym echoing, the balls dropping one after another into small hands. Farah's brother ran the point like he'd been born to it. Ms. Ivanova's rink, Elliot knew, would be frozen by now, a few streets away, and somewhere on it a puck was lifting just off the ice. He blew the whistle and the sound went up toward the rafters and hung there.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius, while porcelain is fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius.
story:
Landon spread newspaper across the kitchen table because his mother had asked him twice already, and because the clay had a way of traveling, a gray dust that found its way into the grain of everything. He was making two pieces for the scholarship portfolio, both due Friday: a shallow earthenware bowl, wide as a dinner plate and still soft enough to dent with a thumb, and a porcelain crane, thin-walled and translucent at the wings, which he had spent three evenings coaxing off the wheel without collapsing it. He turned the crane in the low afternoon light and could see his own fingers through the thinned clay at the shoulder, and he thought, not for the first time, that he loved one piece and trusted the other, and that this was not the same thing.

He had bought the two clays from the same shop, from the same shelf, and had assumed, in the vague way he assumed most things that turned out badly, that clay was clay. He wrapped both pieces in damp cloth and carried the box down the street to Mr. Aquino's garage, where the old kiln sat in the corner like a patient animal and where Mr. Aquino let neighborhood kids fire work for five dollars a load.

Abraham was already there, loading his own mugs onto the shelf, when Landon set the box down and began unwrapping. "You can't put those in together," Abraham said, not unkindly, squinting at the bowl and then at the crane.

"Why not? It's one kiln."

Abraham held up his phone, where he had been reading the studio's firing sheet. "Earthenware fires below about twelve hundred degrees. Porcelain has to go hotter, between twelve hundred and fourteen hundred. Different loads."

Landon looked at the kiln, at the single dial, at the shelf where the mugs sat waiting, and felt the afternoon rearrange itself around a number. The portfolio was due Friday. Mr. Aquino ran one load a week, sometimes two, and only charged for the ones that filled the shelf.

"So I fire the crane and the bowl waits," Landon said.

"Or you fire the bowl and the crane waits. My mugs are taking half the space either way."

Landon wanted to argue, and part of him wanted to equivocate, to suggest that maybe the clays were close enough, that maybe he could squeeze both in and see what happened. But he had heard that tone in his own voice before, usually right before something broke, and he knew it was not curiosity talking but the hope that someone else would absorb the culpability if it went wrong. The crane could slump in a low firing, or the bowl could crack in a high one; either way he would be the one who had known and gambled anyway.

He took both pieces outside to the driveway and set them on the trunk of his car in the last of the light, because it had become a decision that wanted sky over it. He tried to reason it out the way his philosophy teacher had taught him, weighing principles: the crane was the better object, the braver object, the one that showed what he could become. The bowl was the honest object, the one that showed what he was, with its thumbprints still visible along the rim where he had steadied it. He thought about how a portfolio was a claim about the future, and how a claim about the future built out of pretense was worth less than a modest true thing, and then he thought about how that itself might be a pretense, a comfortable story he could tell for choosing the safe piece.

Abraham came out and leaned against the car. "You could fire the crane this week and the bowl next," he said. "After the deadline."

"Then it's not in the portfolio."

"Then it's not in the portfolio."

The diurnal rhythm of the street was winding down, sprinklers ticking off one by one, a dog being called in, and Landon understood that the evening was not going to hand him an answer, only the last of the light to decide by. He picked up the crane, feeling its weightless heat through his palms as if it had already been fired, and then he picked up the bowl, heavier, duller, certain of itself.

"I'll take the bowl," he said. "The crane can wait for next week's load." He carried the bowl back into the garage and set it beside Abraham's mugs on the shelf, and Mr. Aquino closed the kiln door and turned the dial, and through the small dark window Landon watched the elements begin their slow blush toward orange.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: GIS layers stored in different coordinate reference systems will not line up correctly until one is reprojected to match the other.
story:
Justin had thirty-six hours to turn a school project into something that could stop a parking lot from being poured over a floodplain, or at least that was how he phrased it to Greta when she asked why he was still in the computer lab at six o'clock on a Thursday. In reality the project was smaller: overlay the county flood map on the city housing map, find the neighborhoods that sat inside the high-risk zone, and present it to the city council's youth liaison on Saturday morning. Mr. Vu, who supervised the lab the way a cat supervised a garden, had signed the permission form and said only, "Do not embarrass me in front of the liaison." Justin took this as affection.

The lab smelled of whiteboard marker and the vending machine's burnt-coffee breath. Justice had claimed the workstation with the good chair and was eating pretzels with the deliberate calm of someone who had finished his half of the poster already. "You know," he said, "your half is the map. Without the map, my half is a poster about fonts."

"Thank you for that pressure," Justin said. "Very belligerent of you."

"I'm supportive. I'm being supportive with an agenda."

Justin had exported both layers from the city's open data portal that afternoon, and at first the whole thing had worked beautifully, the software humming, the layers stacking like pancakes. Then he'd zoomed in and found the river running through the middle of city hall, then through the elementary school, then, when he zoomed further, directly through the water tower, which was a feat even for a very ambitious river. At home that night he'd stared at it so long his mother had asked whether the map was winning.

Back in the lab he opened the layer properties and read what was there: one layer stored its coordinates in one reference system, the other in another. He knew the words now, had read them twice on the bus with his thumb holding the page. He typed into the search bar, found the reproject option, and let the software do it. When the screen redrew, the river slid sideways like a curtain being pulled straight and settled exactly where the river actually was, along the north edge of the neighborhoods, lapping at the borders of the rental blocks he'd pulled from the housing file.

Greta leaned over his shoulder with a mug of the vending machine coffee, which she drank on principle rather than for pleasure. "So before, the flood was drowning city hall."

"And the water tower. The water tower was underwater. Very metaphysical." He rotated the view. "Look at it now, though. The high-risk zone touches these three blocks, and those blocks have the oldest housing stock in the file. Look at the build dates."

Greta looked. Justice abandoned his pretzels and looked. The oldest houses stood where the water would go, which Justin understood was not a coincidence but also not, by itself, a conclusion. He thought of the unit in geography where Mr. Vu had written determinism on the board and crossed it out, arguing that places shape people but people also argue back, and that any map claiming to know the future should have to raise its hand first.

"That's the story," Justice said, already uncapping a marker. "Old houses, flood zone, done, poster, glory."

"It's not done." Justin highlighted the blocks. "Some of these have been there sixty years and never flooded. The zone is probability, not prophecy. If I say 'these houses are doomed,' I'm lying by a little, and a little is enough for the liaison to dismiss all of it." He pulled up the historical layer Greta had found, the one showing where the creek had been channelized decades ago, and laid it over the flood zone, suturing the three maps together into a single argument: the water used to go somewhere else, people built where it used to go, and now the maps disagreed about how much that mattered.

Mr. Vu drifted over at closing time and studied the screen with his hands in his pockets. "So what do you tell them on Saturday?"

"That the risky blocks are the old ones, and that the city's own data says so," Justin said. "And that anyone who zooms in wrong will think the river runs through city hall, so check the coordinates before you panic." He saved the file twice, then a third time to a thumb drive Greta held out without being asked. Justice began lettering, Greta argued for a blue that didn't look "mournful," and the vending machine dispensed its last coffee with a shudder, like it had opinions about all of them.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Sydney sat in the third row with a spiral notebook open on her knees, trying to make a ten-minute play out of the night her father lost his job. She had not decided to write about that; it had simply arrived on the page when Ms. Mwangi said, write a moment from your own life, and everyone else groaned. Now she had four pages of dialogue between a father and a daughter at a kitchen table, and no idea how to make it stop being a transcript.

Michelle sat two seats over, rehearsing her own script under her breath. Hers was about an eviction, an indigent family in a motel room arguing about whether to keep the cat, and it was good in a way that made Sydney's chest tighten. On stage, Katelyn was running her piece with two boys from drama club, a fight between a mother and a son about college money, and the fight kept ending without ending, the lights coming down on two people still standing in the same positions they had started in.

"That's the third time it just stops," Michelle said, not looking up.

"I know," Katelyn called from the stage. She came down the steps and dropped into the seat in front of them, script folded in her fist. "He yells, she yells, and then I don't know what to do with them. What changed? Nothing changed. That's the whole problem."

Sydney flipped back through her notebook. She had underlined a sentence from the packet Ms. Mwangi had handed out on the first day, mostly unread until now. "In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end," she said. She had meant it as a deflection, something to say instead of admitting she was stuck too, but saying it aloud made her look at her own pages differently. Her kitchen-table scene had a beginning, the father sitting down. It had a middle, the excuses, the daughter pretending to study. It had no end. It had the moment where, in real life, she had gone to her room and put on headphones, and the night had simply continued into the next day.

"So what's your end?" Katelyn asked her, turning around fully.

"I don't have one. That's the thing. It didn't have one."

Ms. Mwangi crossed the stage then, marking tape in her hand, and crouched by the front row to speak with them. She did not lecture. She asked Sydney what the daughter wanted in the scene, and when Sydney said she wanted her father to say it out loud, to say the words, Ms. Mwangi said, "Then decide whether he does, and put that on stage. You can't parametrize it with a lighting cue or a music swell. Something has to be different in the last image than in the first."

From the wings, where she had gone to find her prop cat, Michelle watched the three of them in the third row: Sydney writing fast, Katelyn leaning over the seatback, Ms. Mwangi already moving on toward the sound booth. Michelle had thought her own script was finished, but standing there in the dark she saw its shape differently, the way a bone under an X-ray shows a morphology the skin hides. Her eviction scene began with the cat in a carrier and it ought to end with the carrier empty or the cat gone or someone carrying it out into the hall. Something carried out. Something carried in. She wrote carrier empty in the margin and underlined it twice.

Sydney read her new ending aloud in the empty auditorium an hour later, when the others had gone and the work lights were the only ones on. The father did not say the words. Instead he took off his watch, the one his own father had given him, and set it on the table between them, and the daughter understood it was going to be sold. In real life there had been no watch, no object, no gesture, only the headphones and the door. The stage version was a lie and it was also truer, and she could not have explained the difference to anyone, and she did not need to.

Katelyn came back for her forgotten jacket and stopped in the aisle to listen. When Sydney finished, the pages trembling slightly in her hand, Katelyn clapped once, softly, the way you do in a quiet room.

"So what changed?" Katelyn asked.

"Everything," Sydney said. "Or at least the watch."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: William Appleman Williams's 1959 book The Tragedy of American Diplomacy began the revisionist school, arguing that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War.
story:
The cenotaph sat at the fork of two streets, granite going grey the way teeth go grey, and David sat on its bottom step with two library books beside him because Mr. Tremblay had said the assignment could not be done from one side. On the left was the orthodox account, a thick history that explained the Cold War as a reaction to Soviet moves. On the right was a slimmer book, and David had found it first not in the library but in his grandfather's spare room, wedged under a domino set in a drawer that smelled of pipe tobacco. He had taken it down expecting a dedication or an inscription, something that would tell him why a man who had served kept a book that seemed to argue against everything he had fought for.

"They're not going to fight you," Joseph said, dropping onto the step beside him with two coffees, handing one over without being asked. "The books. They're not going to fight you."

"They kind of are," David said. "My grandfather has this one. The Tragedy of American Diplomacy. It came out in 1959, this guy William Appleman Williams, and it basically started the whole revisionist school."

"Meaning what?"

"Meaning historians who said we helped cause it. That American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War." David turned the book over in his hands. "My grandfather kept it for sixty years. He either hated it or he couldn't stop thinking about it."

Juliet came down the path from the bus stop with her scarf pulled over her chin, saw the coffees, and took Joseph's out of his hands without breaking stride. Joseph let her. "You're doing the Tremblay essay at a war memorial," she said. "That's either respect or a threat."

"I'm doing it where it's quiet," David said. "And where the names are." Behind them the panel of names ran in sedimentary rows, layer after layer of engraved letters, war beneath war beneath war, the oldest at the bottom like the oldest stone.

He read aloud for a while, the orthodox historian first, then a page of Williams, and Juliet kept score in the margin of her notebook with little ticks, and it became clear that the two accounts didn't merely disagree about details but about what counted as evidence at all. One treated American actions as responses; the other treated them as a pattern, the same shape recurring in different countries. "So how do you weigh it?" Juliet asked. "They're not even using the same scale."

"That's the problem," David said. "I keep wanting one of them to be lying, because then it's easy. But I don't think either of them is lying. I think I have to decide what the facts are evidence for, and the facts don't come with labels." He looked up at the names. "My grandfather never talked like either of them. He talked about specific places and specific people. Maybe that's a third way of knowing."

Joseph had been quiet longer than usual, and it was Joseph, not David, who noticed that the cold had gotten into Juliet's hands; she was holding the coffee more than drinking it, pressing warmth into her palms. He unwound his own scarf, the long grey one his mother knitted every winter, and looped it around her neck without a word, and she pulled it up over her chin the way she'd had her own, and said "thanks" so quietly the word barely left her.

From where Joseph sat, watching his friend argue with the dead, the assignment looked different than it had in the classroom. Mr. Tremblay had warned them against choosing a side for comfort, and Joseph had assumed that meant they should all end up in the cautious middle, but David wasn't doing that. David was building something stranger: a position that said the orthodox account explained the fear and Williams's book explained the pattern, and that a person could hold both only by admitting, out loud, that he couldn't verify the veracity of either from where he stood, sixty years on, with a library card and a grandfather's silence. Joseph thought most kids would have hidden that gap. David kept pointing at it.

"You should write it exactly like that," Joseph said. "The part where you said you can't verify it. Don't smooth it over."

"Tremblay might want a conclusion."

"Tremblay wants the good ones to problematize the question," Juliet said, tapping her pen on the notebook. "That's the word he used in September. Not answer it. Problem it."

They packed up as the light went amber, David stacking the books so the library one was on the bottom and his grandfather's on top, spine cracked, the dust of the drawer still faintly on the cover. At the path's edge he stopped and put his hand flat against the granite, below the lowest row of names, where the stone was coldest.

"Mr. Tremblay," he said, "is going to get an essay that ends with a question."

"Good," Juliet said. "Then walk us to the bus."

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements.
story:
Joshua had the swing to himself at nine in the morning, which was the only reason he'd come, dragging his sneakers through the wood chips while he rehearsed the sentence he always fumbled: I'm a motivated self-starter with customer service experience. The playground was where he thought best, and Saturday was his last chance before the interview at the garden center on Monday, because on Monday he would be sitting across a desk from a manager trying not to look at his own hands.

Allison found him there, backpack slung over one shoulder, holding two cans of soda from the machine outside the rec center. She sat on the swing beside his without being asked, which was the arrangement between them, and watched him mouth something at the fence.

"You're doing the thing again," she said. "The practicing thing. You look like you're talking to the hydrangeas."

"I'm talking to Mr. Hughes," Joshua said. "In my head. He asked me yesterday why I want the job and I said, and I'm quoting, 'Because of money reasons.'" He let the swing drift backward until the chains went slack, then forward again. "Two words. One of them was 'reasons.'"

Alix arrived ten minutes later, late because Alix was always late, and dropped onto the merry-go-round with a textbook open in his lap. He'd had three interviews already that summer and gotten two offers, and he'd taken neither, which Allison said was because Alix liked being wanted more than he liked working. Joshua thought that was unkind and also probably true.

"Ask me anything," Joshua said to him. "Pretend you're the manager."

Alix spun the merry-go-round slowly with one heel, considering. "Why do you want to work at Hanley's Garden Center?"

"Because of money reasons."

"See, that's the problem," Alix said. He wasn't unkind about it, which somehow made it worse. "You look at the ground when you answer. My cousin says there's this thing, in a study from 1999, these researchers, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh. They found people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements. Like if you lean forward when they lean forward. Copying, but small, so they don't notice."

"So it's a trick," Allison said.

"It's not a trick, it's a study."

Allison opened her soda with a hiss that seemed to punctuate the whole discussion. "It's a trick if you do it on purpose to get something. If the manager likes you because you moved like a mirror, that's not the manager liking you."

Alix rolled his eyes, but Joshua was quiet, because he'd been mesmerized by the idea, the possibility that there was a mechanism underneath liking, something you could lean on. He thought about Mr. Hughes, who was his neighbor and had coached little league for twenty years and had told him once that the whole game was in your eyes. Mr. Hughes believed you looked people in the eye because that was honest. Alix's study believed you moved the way they moved because it worked. Those weren't the same thing, and Joshua couldn't tell yet whether they could both be true at once.

"Ask me again," he said.

"Why do you want to work at Hanley's?"

Joshua looked up, at Alix this time, not the fence, not the hydrangeas, not his own knuckles. "My grandmother had a garden and I spent whole summers in it, and I know the difference between what a seedling needs and what a full plant needs, and I want money, honestly, because I'm saving for a laptop for school, and I'd be good at the watering question customers always have."

Alix stopped spinning the merry-go-round. Allison was nodding slowly, and the chains of the empty swing creaked in the wind coming off the ball field.

"Now the leaning," Alix said, and leaned forward.

Joshua sat still. He understood that at some point on Monday, if the manager leaned across the desk, he would have to decide in half a second whether to move with them, and he did not know yet what he would do, whether matching a stranger's shoulders was clever or false, whether Mr. Hughes's honesty and Chartrand and Bargh's numbers were enemies or just two different gardens. He knew only that the eye contact he could do, because he had just done it, and it had felt less like a performance than he'd feared.

"Your move," Alix said, still leaning forward, elbows on his knees, waiting.

Joshua planted his sneakers in the wood chips, kept his eyes on Alix's face, and stayed exactly where he was.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
The video arrived at 11:47 on a Tuesday, forwarded from Aydin with three exclamation points and the caption "watch this now." It showed a warehouse fire, smoke boiling out of loading doors, firefighters silhouetted against the glare, and overlaid text claiming the blaze had started that morning at the food distribution center two towns over, where Raphael's aunt had worked for eleven years. He watched it twice, his thumb hovering over the button that would send it to his mother, then to the group chat, then everywhere.

Christopher was already on the couch, shoes off, working through a bag of pretzels. He leaned over Raphael's shoulder, crumbs catching in the weave of the blanket. "That's the place off Route 9," he said. "My cousin unloads trucks there." On the screen the fire licked at the diaphanous plastic sheeting over the loading dock, melting it into long ribbons that curled and fell.

Raphael's first instinct was speed. The video had forty thousand shares and the comments were already a bonfire of their own, people demanding answers from the company, someone claiming a friend's shift had started at dawn and no one had heard from her. Every minute he hesitated, the thing traveled further without him. He opened the image search on his phone and dragged the video file into the box, the way he'd once checked a photo of a "rare double rainbow" that turned out to be from a stock site. The engine thought about it, then refused. It wanted a picture, not a moving thing. "It won't take video," he said, and the words came out more like an accusation than information.

Christopher suggested texting Aydin back and asking where he got it. Aydin's reply came in four seconds: "saw it on my feed, share it, people need to know." That did nothing to assuage the pressure in Raphael's chest, the feeling that withholding the clip was a kind of cowardice, a failure of loyalty to his aunt and to everyone else's aunts. The comments kept climbing. He refreshed the page and watched the number go up by three hundred in the time it took to blink.

Then he remembered something Ms. Yang had said in September, not as a lecture, just in passing while collecting essays: that most of what passes for news on a phone is a costume. He sat with that for a second, thumbs stilled. If the engine wanted an image, he could make images. He paused the video where the smoke column was sharpest against the sky and took a screenshot. Then he scrubbed forward to the frame with the collapsed awning and took another, and a third from the end, where a firefighter stood alone in front of the gutted doors. He fed the first screenshot into the image search and waited, the phone warm in his hand, pretzel dust on the screen.

The results loaded slowly, one tile at a time, and the tensest part was how ordinary they looked. A photography contest entry from another country. A news article. Another news article. He opened the second one and read the date, then read it again because the number refused to arrange itself into sense. The fire was real, the warehouse was real, but it had burned years ago, in a town he'd never heard of, and the loading doors in the article were unmistakably the same doors, the same awning, the same single firefighter with his helmet under his arm. Whoever made the video had dressed an old disaster in new clothes and pointed it at their distribution center off Route 9, and forty thousand people, maybe more by now, were furious at a company that had done nothing this morning at all.

He typed it out to Aydin: the clip was old, from somewhere else, and he had the screenshots to prove it. He pasted the link. He started typing a longer explanation, something about how a video can't be searched the way a picture can, so you have to catch it standing still, frame by frame, and ask the frames where they've been, and then he deleted most of it because it sounded like a term paper. "Check the frames before you share," he sent instead. Aydin's reply was a single thumbs-up, and then, a minute later, the confession that he'd already sent it to his mother, who had sent it to her whole book club.

Christopher reached over and ate the last pretzel.
