"So nobody's aunt is in danger," he said, and Raphael said no, nobody's aunt, not today, and felt the strange flatness of a disaster that had never existed. He was about to close the article when a new comment appeared under the video, from the company itself, dated four minutes ago: "We are aware of a circulating video and can confirm no incident has occurred at our facility. We are investigating its origin." Then a second comment, right below it, from a user with a fish emoji for a profile picture: "That's exactly what they'd say."

Raphael watched the replies to that comment begin.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
story:
Ms. Takahashi had pushed the desks into a circle, which in her classroom meant either a debate or a catastrophe, and by fourth period Brianna had learned to tell the difference by how quietly the marker smelled. Today the whiteboard said ELECTION DAY in letters so large they seemed to be compensating for something, and beneath it, in smaller print, POLLS CLOSE AT SEVEN. It was 10:14 in the morning. Brianna turned eighteen two Saturdays ago, which meant she was the only person in the room who could actually do anything about the thing they had been arguing about for six weeks.

"You registered at your mom's address," Cailyn said, leaning across the gap between desks. "You could just not go. Nobody would know."

"Twelve people in this room would know," Brianna said. "Thirteen, counting Ms. Takahashi."

Elijah, who sat by the window and treated opinions like legal evidence, leaned back until his chair creaked. "You realize your one vote has never decided anything in the history of this county. Statistically you'd have more influence standing outside the fire station yelling."

"That's not the unit of measurement," Brianna said, and then heard herself, and stopped.

Ms. Takahashi, who had a policy of not rescuing students mid-argument, wrote DISCERNMENT on the board without turning around. "For your essays," she said. "Due Friday. Which is after today, in case anyone is confused about deadlines."

The essay had been assigned in September, when Brianna still thought she knew how she'd vote. Her mother's position could be summarized as a single sentence delivered over dishes, something about the school board candidate who wanted to cut the arts budget, delivered with the flat finality of a verdict. Her father disagreed, not loudly, but with the small persistent logic he used on crossword puzzles: taxes, schedules, ancillary costs, things Brianna had never once thought about. She had intended to sit down Thursday night, write the essay, vote the essay, and be finished. Instead she had written nothing, because every time she started, her sentences turned into two people talking past each other, both of them sounding like her.

At lunch, in the emptying cafeteria, Cailyn pulled up a photo of the sample ballot on her phone. "Why does it look like a test? Like a Scantron from hell."

"That's the Australian ballot," Elijah said, in his evidence voice. Brianna looked at him. "It's actually called the Australian ballot," he went on, "because the Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856. Printed, secret, standardized. We borrowed it."

"That's the one part of today that makes sense," Brianna said. "Nobody's allowed to see how you mark it. Not your mom, not the poll workers, not your teacher." She thought of the circle of desks, of Ms. Takahashi writing words on boards that would be erased by the janitor at nine. Something about the secret printed page steadied her, though she couldn't have said why, and she didn't try to in front of Cailyn.

The fire station smelled like floor wax and someone's microwaved lunch. A woman with a clipboard found Brianna's name, made her sign, and handed her a paper sleeve and a blue pen. The booth was a cardboard stand-up, the kind of thing that would not survive a strong wind, with a tiny pencil shelf. Brianna stood there for four minutes. The school board race was at the bottom, below the county commissioner and a referendum she had genuinely researched. Her mother's voice ran through her head, then her father's, and neither one eviscerated the other, which was the annoying thing; both of them were mostly right about different halves of the question. She marked the school board race one way, the referendum the other, and let herself feel no triumph about either. The page fed into the scanner with a sound like a card being shuffled into a deck.

Outside, the light was going amber over the parking lot. Elijah was leaning against the bike rack as though he had been there all afternoon, though he lived nowhere near this polling place. "So?" he said.

"So nothing's resolved," Brianna said. "I voted anyway."

He nodded slowly, as if this were data. "The essay's still due Friday."

"I know when it's due," she said, and started walking, and behind her, faintly, the fire station doors swung shut.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parallel parking, a driver usually reverses in from alongside the car in front, turning the wheel toward the curb first and then away as the car swings into the space.
story:
Laurie had told her mother she was doing laundry, which was true the way most of her statements were true lately, containing a fact wrapped around an omission. The bags she carried into the Riverside Laundromat held three weeks of clothes and, folded flat between two towels, the driver's manual she had borrowed from Mr. Sato, the neighbour who lived two doors down and had once, in another life she was fairly sure, been a driving instructor. She was certain about that. She was less certain whether she had asked him for help or whether he had offered, but either way he was meeting her here at four, when the place emptied out and the parking lot in front went unused.

She loaded the machines first, because laundry was the official project, and sat on the folding table with the manual open to the chapter on parallel parking. The photographs showed a car slipping neatly between two others, arrows curving like the paths of birds. She read the same paragraph four times. Something about turning toward the curb and then away, the words rearranging themselves every time she looked. She decided she understood it. She was, she'd told Camilla at school on Thursday, basically ready for the test, and Camilla had said "basically" back to her in a voice that Laurie chose to interpret as admiration.

Mr. Sato arrived at four with a thermos and his own set of keys, holding them up like a small trophy. "The Buick," he said. "My wife is at her sister's until Sunday. We have the lot until she isn't." He was smaller than she remembered, or possibly she had grown, and he moved around the car checking the tires with an unhurried thoroughness that made her think of the penurious years he must have lived through, saving things, keeping the Buick alive long past the age when other men traded up.

The lot had two faded lines painted near the curb, and he stood a shopping cart in front of one to serve as the car she'd be parking behind. "Reverse in from alongside," he said, and nothing more, folding his arms. She pulled up beside the cart, checked her mirrors twice because checking twice seemed like the kind of thing a good driver did, and began to back. She turned the wheel toward the curb and held it there, waiting for the magic, and the Buick swung in and kept swinging until she was parked at an angle so steep that the front bumper pointed hopefully at the laundromat's plate glass window.

"I turned toward the curb," she said, gripping the wheel. "The book said."

"First," Mr. Sato said. He tapped the glass with one knuckle. "Toward the curb first. Then away, as the car swings into the space. When your rear wheel is where you want it, straighten, then turn back the other way. You held the turn too long. You only get the first half."

She pulled out and tried again, telling herself she was not embarrassed, that embarrassment was an affectation she refused to perform, and believing it almost completely. This time she reversed in from alongside the cart, turned toward the curb, watched her mirror until the rear corner of the space came around, then turned away, and the Buick settled against the curb so gently she felt it through the seat before she saw it. Straight. Level. She sat with her hands still on the wheel, not wanting to move in case moving ruined it.

"So it's two turns," she said. "Not one."

"It's knowing when the second one comes," he said, and got out and moved the shopping cart a foot closer, because the space was now generous and he was not a generous man with parking spaces.

They drove after that. He directed her onto the highway ramp three blocks over, and merging was a different animal, one requiring speed instead of patience, and she merged badly the first time and properly the second, a semi somewhere behind them laying on the horn in a way that failed to metastasize into the catastrophe she'd braced for. When they returned, the dryers had almost finished their cycle, and through the window she could see her clothes turning over and over, all of them, keeping their colors.

Later, alone at the folding table, she caught herself telling Camilla the story by text and typing the words "nailed it first try," and she looked at them for a long moment before her thumbs did what they wanted anyway, and the message went, and the warm shirts smelled like her mother's detergent.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: In Bastiat's broken-window parable, money spent replacing a window could otherwise have bought shoes or a book, so the breakage creates no net gain.
story:
The mall on a Saturday afternoon had the particular noise of everyone wanting something at once, and Alexis moved through it with sixty dollars folded in his pocket and no decision made. He had earned it over three weekends of bagging groceries, and for three weekends he had let himself ruminate on the choice: the used copy of the racing game Porter kept raving about, or the gray sneakers in the window of the shoe store near the food court, the ones with the cracked soles of his current pair staring up at him every morning as evidence of the need.

He found Porter and Addison at a table outside the pretzel stand. Porter was holding court, as he did, retelling a story about his cousin's car. "Somebody backed into the fender last week," Porter said, tearing off a piece of pretzel. "Honestly, best thing that could've happened. The shop downtown got a whole day of work out of it. That's money moving, that's jobs. My uncle says accidents like that keep the economy going."

Addison rolled her eyes so far Alexis worried for her. "That's the broken window thing," she said. "You break a window, the glazier gets paid, and you say the economy won. But the money spent replacing the window could have bought shoes or a book. The breakage creates no net gain. It's a parable. Bastiat. We read it in econ."

"It's a French guy," Addison said. "And no, that's not the point. You're counting what the shop got and forgetting what the cousin lost, which is the exact same money and a fender he already had."

Porter opened his mouth, closed it, and redirected his energy into his pretzel. Alexis stood there feeling something shift, small but tectonic, the way an argument can reorganize what you thought you already knew. Because he had been doing a version of Porter's math all afternoon without noticing. Sixty dollars spent on the game meant evenings with Porter and Addison, laughing, competing, belonging. Sixty dollars spent on the shoes meant dry socks in November and no more jokes from the guys in the locker room about duct tape. Both purchases looked like gains from where he stood, and only from where he stood. What he hadn't been willing to look at was the other side of each: the game bought at the price of the shoes, the shoes bought at the price of the game, and no clever argument that made both appear in his pocket at once.

He wandered toward the shoe store and stood at the window. Mr. Morningstar, who had run the place since Alexis was small enough to press his nose against the glass, came out with a broom. "Those ones again," he said, nodding at the gray sneakers. "Third time this month you've stood there."

"Third and a half," Alexis admitted.

"You know I can hold them till Tuesday. Not forever. Tuesday."

Inside, Alexis tried them on. They fit the way shoes fit in stories, perfectly, and he walked a lap around the rack in them feeling like a slightly improved version of himself. The tag said fifty-eight. He took them off slowly, set them back in the box, and carried the box to the counter, where he then stood doing nothing with his hand on his wallet.

"Problem?" Mr. Morningstar asked.

"There's a game," Alexis said. "That's all. There's a game, and there's these, and I only have the one sixty." He heard how it sounded, a rich kid's complaint, and hurried on. "It's not a real problem. It's just that whichever one I pick, the other one's gone. That's the whole thing I keep tripping over. People talk like choosing is free."

Mr. Morningstar rang up the sale and paused before bagging them. "My father drove a truck for thirty years," he said. "Every load he took was a load he didn't take. He never called that a tragedy. He called it Tuesday."

Alexis paid, and the bills left his pocket with a finality that surprised him, like a door that only opened one way. He carried the bag out past the pretzel stand, where Addison was still sitting, working through a history study guide with her headphones half on. He sat down across from her and pulled out his phone to text Porter, typing and deleting twice before he landed on it.

"Tell your uncle the fender money bought him a story and nothing else," he wrote. Then he set the phone face down and looked at his bag, at the sharp corner of the shoebox pressing through the paper. "I'll have the game money again by the end of the month," he said, partly to Addison and partly to the bag. "Probably. I don't actually know that yet."

Addison pulled one headphone off. "You could rent it," she said, and pointed her pen at the game store across the aisle.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In his 1979 book The Imperative of Responsibility, Hans Jonas proposed the rule: 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life.'
story:
The fluorescent lights above the auditorium stage hummed at a pitch only Alexander seemed able to hear, though at the moment he had bigger problems, the chief one being that his debate partner had the flu and his opponent was Asia Okonkwo, who had not lost a round all season. The resolution was printed on the sheet in his shaking hand: that the school board should approve a pilot program putting experimental AI tutors in every classroom by fall.

He had drawn the negative, which surprised him, because privately he wanted the tutors. His calculus grade had been clawed back from a cliff by exactly such software, and he felt something close to gratitude toward it. Loyalty, though, was not the assignment. The assignment was to argue that a technology with no track record should not be placed in front of fourteen hundred students, and he had spent the week assembling evidence about algorithmic bias and data privacy while feeling like a hypocrite in a diaphanous disguise, one his opponents could see through whenever they cared to look.

"Point of information," Asia said in the first cross-examination, leaning into the microphone. "Every technology was once experimental. Pencils had a first day too. If your standard is certainty before deployment, you've exonerated nothing and prevented everything. Isn't the responsible position to test carefully rather than refuse entirely?"

"Testing is fine," Alexander said. "Testing on my entire grade without asking my entire grade isn't." He heard Darwin, sitting third row with his debate notebook, mutter something that sounded like hold that line.

But the round turned in the second hour, during open questioning, when a freshman in the audience stood up. She was small and very serious, and she said, "Everyone keeps talking about us. Who speaks for the people who aren't born yet? The ones who'll live with whatever we decide?"

The auditorium went quiet in the way rooms do when someone has asked a question no one prepared for. Asia glanced at her flowsheet. The moderator checked his watch. Alexander's mind went blank, and then, from somewhere in the reading he'd done at two in the morning while avoiding his calculus problem set, something surfaced. He had found it in a footnote, chased it to the library, and read it twice without understanding why it stuck.

"In 1979," he said, standing, "Hans Jonas wrote a book called The Imperative of Responsibility." He could feel his voice steadying as the words arrived. "His rule was: 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life.' It's a kind of categorical imperative for technology. The old ethics asked whether your act harms your neighbor. This one asks whether your act, multiplied and compounded across generations, leaves genuine human life possible at all."

Asia did not attack it. She wrote something down, and when her rebuttal came she argued, cleanly and without mockery, that Jonas's rule could justify the tutors rather than forbid them: education sustained human life; therefore a tool that educated more people better passed the test, not failed it. It was a good move, and Alexander recognized it as one he should have made first. He had handed her a sword and watched her take the advantage with it.

The judges split two to one, for her. Afterward, in the corridor by the vending machines, Darwin clapped him on the shoulder and said the freshman's question had won him the crowd even if it lost him the round. Mr. Chan, who coached the team and disapproved of displays of temperament, had watched from the back and said nothing, which from him was praise. "You quoted an actual philosopher," Darwin said. "She quoted you back at yourself. That's the game, unfortunately."

Alexander was still holding his flowsheet, creased now into a triangle, when Asia came out with her bag over her shoulder. "Good round," she said. "For what it's worth, I think the tutors are probably a mistake. I just think you were wrong about why." He laughed, and she waited, half-turned toward the exit, as if she expected him to argue it, and he stood there in the humming light, holding the losing side of a case he still believed in, having said nothing when the bell for the vote rang down the hall.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Sikh gurdwara's langar serves free vegetarian meals to anyone regardless of religion, caste or status, and people traditionally eat together seated on the floor as equals.
story:
Cole had promised Farrah he would show her the gurdwara during the Vaisakhi celebration, and he regretted the promise the whole drive there, in the way you regret something that is already done and cannot be taken back. His mother sat in the passenger seat directing him around a detour, and Farrah sat in the back with her hands folded on her knees, which was strange, because Farrah never folded her hands anywhere. She argued with referees. She had once told a substitute teacher that his worksheet was beneath everyone's dignity. Now she was quiet, watching the storefronts give way to the flat alluvial fields at the edge of town, and Cole could not tell whether the quiet was respect or fear.

"Will I be allowed in?" she asked as they parked. "Like, actually allowed?"

"Anyone's allowed." He heard how flat it came out, like a rule he was reciting, so he tried again. "You'll see."

Inside the community hall the smell reached them first, ghee and cardamom and something under that, onions going soft in a huge pot. His grandmother was already in the kitchen, her dupatta pulled forward, and she waved him over without pausing her stirring. She asked who the girl was. Cole tried to verbalize it in Punjabi and failed halfway, falling into English, and his grandmother looked at Farrah for a long moment and then said, "Tell her to eat," which was, Cole understood, the entire verdict.

Farrah had questions, and she asked them in a low voice while they stood against the wall. Was there a fee, was there a sign-up, did she have to say she believed something. Cole kept shaking his head, and each shake felt inadequate, so finally he said, "It's called langar. There's no charge, there's no list. It doesn't matter what you are." He gestured at the hall. "Look who's here." She looked. There was a man in a suit who had clearly come from some office, two students in sweatshirts, an old woman from the care home up the road whose religion nobody knew, the guy who pumped gas at the station on Route 9, all of them drifting toward the same doorway.

But it was the floor that stopped her. In the main hall, rows of people sat cross-legged on the woven mats, and volunteers moved between them with steel buckets, doling out dal and rice onto every plate in turn. Farrah stood at the threshold with her tray and did not move. "Everyone sits down?" she said. "The suit guy too?"

"He's already sitting. Third row." It was true, the man from the office had his shoes off at the door like everyone else, his briefcase under the coat rack, and he was eating with his hands awkwardly, learning as he went, and nobody was watching him learn.

They found space near his grandmother's friend from the seamstress shop, and a teenage volunteer Cole vaguely knew from district math competitions knelt and served them both without asking who was who. Farrah ate slowly. She was trying, Cole could see, to fit the thing into a category she already owned, the way she filed protests and fundraisers, and the thing kept not fitting. "So it's charity," she said at last.

"It's not exactly charity." He did not want to explain it badly. He thought of his grandmother's line of the house in her village, and the stories about which people had once been expected to eat apart from which other people, and how the floor here flattened all of it, but he could not get the history to sit still long enough to say it. "It's more like, nobody's above anybody here. On the floor there's no way to be." Farrah considered this with her spoon halfway to her mouth, and then she said, "That's harder than it sounds," and Cole, who had spent years failing to say out loud what she had just said in seven words, agreed that it was.

They went back for seconds, which Farrah did boldly, holding out her plate to the volunteer the way she held out arguments in class, chin first. On their way out they passed Ms. Chan, his tenth-grade English teacher, waiting in the line with a covered dish she had evidently brought as an offering of some kind, looking uncertain where to set it down. Farrah, without any hesitation, took the dish from her hands and carried it to the kitchen counter, and Ms. Chan said, "Thank you, I wasn't sure," and Farrah said, "Nobody here is sure, that's the whole point," and Cole laughed before he could stop himself. In the doorway he paused to retrieve his shoes and found his grandmother's alongside them, plain rubber slippers, set down in the same row as the office man's polished leather ones, and he stood there a moment with his own shoe in his hand, looking at the row.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A deductive argument is called sound only when it is valid and all of its premises are actually true, so a sound argument's conclusion must be true.
story:
The ceiling fan in Ms. Girma's classroom ticked like a metronome set too slow, and Stella had copied the debate resolution onto her notebook three times as if repetition would sharpen it. Resolved: that the school should fund a later bus route. She was arguing for it, which she believed, which was the problem. Believing made her sloppy.

"You're proselytizing," Belle said, dropping into the chair beside her and cracking open a granola bar. "You keep preaching instead of proving." Belle wanted the affirmative to lose, cleanly and publicly, because losing to her would look good on the record for captain selection in May, and she had said so, twice, without apology.

Maximus sat across the room with his legal pad, phlegmatic as ever, his pen moving in small economical strokes. He was her opponent, and he had an argument he kept reciting like a prayer. All policies that increase district spending should be rejected. The later bus route increases district spending. Therefore the later bus route should be rejected. Stella had heard it in practice rounds and each time felt the floor tilt under her without being able to say why.

"Run it again," she said, and he did, tapping each line with the pen.

She tried attacking the conclusion. Students need the route; her brother worked closing shifts at the pharmacy and walked home in the dark along Marsh Road. Maximus nodded, unmoved, and repeated the syllogism. She tried attacking the word "should," and Ms. Girma, watering the spider plant by the window with her back half turned, said only, "That's not where it's weak."

The fan ticked. Stella laid the argument out on her own page in her own handwriting, and it looked strange there, like a borrowed coat. The shape of it held. If the first line were true, the second true, then the last line followed the way water follows a channel. Nothing wrong with the plumbing. So she went looking at what was flowing through it, premise by premise, and stopped at the first one. All policies that increase district spending should be rejected. The district had increased spending last year for the new gym floor, and Maximus had written an editorial praising it. She raised her hand.

"His argument's valid," she said, when Ms. Girma turned around, "but the first premise is just false. He doesn't even believe it."

"Say the whole word," Maximus said, not unkindly. He was flipping back through his legal pad to the editorial, his jaw tightening, the pen still in his hand. "What's it called when it's valid and the premises are true?"

"Sound," Stella said. "It's only sound when it's valid and the premises are actually true. Yours isn't."

The room went quiet in a way that had weight. Belle had stopped chewing. Ms. Girma set the watering can down on the sill and said nothing, which was her way of saying everything. Maximus read his own editorial in silence, his finger under the line where he had called the gym floor spending "an investment any serious program requires," and the bell was four minutes away, and the round was tomorrow.

"So I fix the premise," he said finally, and began writing, crossing out, rewriting, and Stella understood that beating him once would not be beating him. She looked down at her own notes, at her brother's dark walk home, at the resolution she still believed in, and realized she didn't yet have an argument of her own that would survive the same inspection she'd just performed on his. Belle leaned over and read her page and raised one eyebrow, a challenge and almost a gift.

"Four minutes," Belle said, tapping the clock. "Build one."

Stella turned to a clean sheet and wrote: If a policy serves students the district is responsible for, then cost alone cannot reject it. She looked at it a long time, hearing the fan, smelling chalk and overripe banana from someone's lunch in the wastebasket, and did not yet know if the second half was true.

"Timer," said Ms. Girma, and started it.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: In The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in 1856, Alexis de Tocqueville argued the Revolution continued the centralization of power already begun under the French monarchy.
story:
Jeremy had promised himself he would draft the essay before the weekend ended, and he had honored this promise in the way of most promises made at eleven on a Thursday night: the laptop was open, the cursor blinking at the top of an empty page titled Historiography: The French Revolution Since 1800, and he was sitting in his grandfather's kitchen eating the last of the plum cake. Ms. Popal had assigned it with terrible cheerfulness. "You are not writing about the Revolution," she had said. "You are writing about how people have written about the Revolution. Two hundred years of people changing their minds. Try to keep up."

His grandfather lived in a narrow brick house that smelled of newsprint and vinegar, and Jeremy had been sent there for the weekend on grounds that were never fully explained, possibly related to a bathroom renovation, possibly not. He had brought the laptop, two library books, and a printout of a historiography so dense it read less like scholarship than a morass of footnotes in which earlier historians had drowned one by one. There were Marxists who saw class struggle, revisionists who impugned the whole idea that 1789 was a rupture at all, romantics who mourned the king, and at least one scholar who seemed primarily interested in Napoleon's hats. Jeremy had no thesis. He had plum cake.

"The French Revolution," he announced to the kitchen, because his grandfather had wandered in and it felt rude to say nothing. "Since 1800. How views of it have changed."

"Ah," his grandfather said, in the tone of a man being told about weather. He poured coffee and sat down across from Jeremy in a way that suggested he intended to stay.

"Everyone argues about whether it was a break or a continuation," Jeremy said. "That's the whole fight, basically. Tocqueville said it was a continuation. In The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in 1856, he argued the Revolution just kept going with the centralization of power the monarchy had already begun. Same machine, new drivers." His grandfather's spoon stopped halfway to the cup. Jeremy noticed this and filed it away, the way you notice a door left open in a house where all doors are usually shut.

"I wrote on that," his grandfather said finally. "In 1961. Same question, more or less. Wound up with a third."

"A third?"

"Out of a first. I failed it, Jeremy. First failure of my life, and the last essay I ever wrote." He said this without drama, the way he said most things, and carried his coffee into the other room, and Jeremy sat with the plum cake and the blinking cursor and the strange sensation of having stepped on a floorboard that sounded hollow.

The book was in the sideboard, which Jeremy had no business opening, except that his grandfather had left the sideboard door ajar, which in that house amounted to an engraved invitation. The Old Regime and the Revolution, an English edition, the spine gone soft, and the margins full of a young man's handwriting, the same handwriting as the label on the coffee tin but younger, more certain of itself. Alongside a passage about administrative centralization the note read: buildings tell you this. They kept the ministries. New flag over the old offices. The irony is that nobody wanted to admit it. Further down, in the same hand: the marker's whole argument was sentimental, hedonistic almost, drunk on the drama of the guillotine, blind to the paperwork. The remark was underlined twice. In the back cover, folded flat, was the marked essay. C. Familiar material summarized; no position of your own. See me.

Jeremy recognized the phrase. Ms. Popal had used it on his last paper, word for word, the "no position of your own," and he had assumed it was an original cruelty rather than an inheritance, part of the long centralization of teacherly disapproval, passed down through the offices. He sat on the floor of the sideboard room with a sixty-year-old failed essay on his knees and understood that his grandfather had found the thing and then, apparently, been told it wasn't enough, and had never written anything again, not a letter to a paper, not a memoir, nothing, a whole silence with a C at the bottom of it.

At the kitchen table he opened a blank document and began again, without the library books. Marxists, then revisionists, then back to Tocqueville; the pendulum, the argument nobody finishes. The grandfather's note was right about the buildings and the paperwork, and the marker was right that a summary is not a position, and both of those things could be true at once, and the essay had to hold them without pretending one dissolved the other. Somewhere in the middle of the second paragraph he heard the other room's radio come on, very low, and knew his grandfather was listening through the wall to the sound of typing.

At supper his grandfather asked, not looking up from his plate, whether the old book had been any use.

"It argued with me the whole way through," Jeremy said.

"Good," his grandfather said, and passed him the bread.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Children accounted for about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, according to Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report.
story:
The clipboard said six hampers before lunch, and Nicole had assembled four of them wrong. She had told Ms. Mendoza, when she signed in that morning, that she had done this before, at her old school in Ottawa, which was true in the sense that she had once carried boxes into a gym for an hour and then gone out for poutine with Elianna. She had let the rest of the implication stand on its own, the way you leave a door half open so nobody notices you never walked through it.

"Diapers go on the bottom," Tyra said, not unkindly. Tyra had been there since September, apparently, every Saturday, and knew where the formula was kept and which shelves held the dented cans that had to be checked. "Cereal on top, so nothing crushes it. You've done this before, right?"

Nicole said that she had, and reached for another box of rice. It was easier to prevaricate than to admit she had chosen this place because her mother had said, over dinner in March, that volunteering would look good on applications, and because Nicole had wanted something to put in the personal statement that made her sound like a person she was not yet sure she was. That was the subtlety she kept turning over: the line between doing a good thing for a bad reason and doing it anyway, which her philosophy teacher would have said was no line at all, and which Nicole suspected was the only line that mattered.

A boy came in around eleven with his mother, maybe five years old, in a dinosaur jacket that was too small for him. Nicole watched from behind the counter while Ms. Mendoza logged them in. The mother kept her eyes on the form. The boy looked at the shelves the way Nicole looked at the bakery case at the grocery store, with a concentration that had nothing pleading in it, just inventory. He said something to his mother and she said, "Yes, tomorrow," and Nicole understood that tomorrow was a word that could be a meal.

In Ottawa, in the winter, Elianna had wanted them to skip fourth period and hand out sandwiches downtown, and Nicole had said she had a chemistry test, which was also true, and had watched Elianna go alone through the glass doors with a paper bag under each arm. Nicole had gotten an A. She had thought about that A more since September than she had thought about it when she received it, which suggested something about what grades were actually worth that she was not ready to write down.

"Look at this," Tyra said after the boy and his mother left, holding up a printed page someone had taped inside the packing station cupboard. Nicole leaned over. It was a page from a report, a chart with a bar she followed with her finger. "One in three," Tyra said. "Kids. Children accounted for about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025. That's from HungerCount, the Food Banks Canada report." She said it flatly, like reading a bus schedule, but she read it twice.

Nicole counted the hampers she had packed that morning. Nine, and seven of them had the small jars of puree or the snack packs or the formula tucked in the corner, which she had noticed without noticing, the way you notice weather. She had assumed, before, in the abstract way she assumed most things, that food banks were mostly for men who lived alone, or elderly people, some category that did not include anyone in a dinosaur jacket. One-third. She looked at the bin of Graduates pasta pickups, the little plastic tubs with the toddler on the label, and it seemed suddenly like evidence of a whole country she had driven through without looking at the windows.

She thought about calling Elianna, and did not, and knew that was its own choice, and could not yet say whether it was a bad one. Maybe the honest position was this: she had come here to decorate her own future and found herself useful anyway, and both things were true, and neither cancelled the other out, and she would have to keep checking, week after week, whether she was still doing the work or only doing the story of the work. Ms. Mendoza would have told her not to be so hard on herself. Nicole was not sure she was being hard enough.

At one o'clock a woman came in with a stroller and a girl asleep inside it, and asked, in a voice pitched low so as not to wake her, whether there was any of the apple sauce with no sugar added. Nicole knew exactly where it was. She got two jars, and then, because there was room in the box and because the report page was still open in her mind, a third.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant does not have to sign a new one; the tenancy continues month to month automatically on the same terms.
story:
The line at the bank moved in small, patient shuffles, and Eli stood behind his grandfather with two leases printed out and folded into quarters, one in each back pocket like cards he hadn't decided how to play. The first apartment, on Claremont Street, was nine hundred and fifty a month plus hydro, which the listing swore was cheap. The second was eleven hundred "all inclusive," a phrase Eli had begun to distrust the way he distrusted the word "cozy." He wanted to know which one actually cost less by October, when the first cold snap would arrive and the heating line on the bill would start to climb like something waking up.

"You're doing the thing with your mouth," his grandfather said without turning around. "The thinking thing. Your mother does it too."

"I'm trying to figure out utilities. The first place is sixty dollars cheaper but I have to pay hydro separately, and I don't know what hydro costs in winter."

"Then find out. Ask somebody who's lived through an Ontario January. It's not a riddle, it's arithmetic with weather in it."

Two weeks earlier, his mother had come home from the building on Rosemere with a letter in her hand and her coat still buttoned, which was how he knew it was bad before she said anything. The landlord wanted her to sign a new one-year lease, the letter said, or "arrangements would be reviewed." She had stood in the kitchen twisting the ring she no longer wore and asked Eli, not really asking, whether he thought they should just sign it. He had said yes, obviously, sign it, because a year of certain roof seemed worth any terms. She signed it that night. It was only later, in the third period of a law class he was taking through the college outreach program, that he'd sat up so fast the girl beside him asked if he was okay.

The teacher hadn't explained anything. She had put a scenario on the screen, a tenant whose fixed-term lease was ending, a landlord pressing for a new one-year commitment, and asked the class what the tenant's options were. People guessed: move out, sign, negotiate. Then a woman in the front row, older than everyone, a returning student, said it plainly. "In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant doesn't have to sign a new one. The tenancy continues month to month automatically, on the same terms." Eli had written it in his notebook and then, quietly appalled, boxed it. His mother hadn't needed to sign. She could have stayed, month to month, holding her freedom in one hand instead of handing it over for a calendar year. He hadn't known, and his not-knowing had cost them something, though he couldn't say exactly what. He was still working out whether it exonerated him, the not-knowing, or whether it was just an excuse shaped like one.

At the teller's window now, his grandfather conducted his business with the unhurried authority of a man who had been coming to this branch since it had different carpet. Eli drifted toward the row of desks where a young banker sat behind a nameplate and a chunk of black rock he'd noticed on the way in, glossy and fine-grained, the kind his grade nine science teacher would have called igneous, cooled fast from something that had once been molten. Eli found himself wondering whether the banker had chosen it or inherited it, and whether anyone who chose an igneous paperweight for a desk where people came to negotiate mortgages was making a joke he wasn't getting.

"Those are falling out of your pockets," a voice said. Kiera from his law class was sitting in the waiting chairs with a deposit slip and a paper cup of coffee. "You're the month-to-month guy. You went full exclamation point when that woman said it."

"I didn't go full exclamation point."

"You boxed it in your notes. I saw you." She nodded at the folded pages. "Is that why you're doing all this, the leases?"

He sat down beside her and spread both listings on the armrest between them. "Partly. The Claremont place ends its term in June. If I sign it, and the term ends, I don't have to sign again. It just goes month to month on the same terms. Automatically." Saying it out loud, he heard how it landed, like a small door opening sideways out of a wall. "So the real question isn't which one's cheaper in July. It's which one's cheaper in my second winter, when I have the option to leave and they can't make me stay."

"So price out the hydro," Kiera said, and stole his pen.

They did it on the back of the deposit slip. The banker's estimate for a one-bedroom in an older building was a hundred and ten in the coldest months, averaging out to maybe seventy-five across the year, though he'd said it with a shrug that Eli recognized as honest uncertainty, the kind you couldn't resolve, only budget around. On that arithmetic Claremont still came out ahead by a little, by less than the listing had implied, and less than he'd hoped. He sat with the two numbers side by side and the strange new fact underneath them, that a lease was not a cage but a corridor with doors along it, and that you could walk out of one without ending the walk.

His grandfather came back from the window holding a slip of his own. He looked at the deposit slip covered in Kiera's handwriting, at the folded leases, at Eli. "You found out what a winter costs?"

"Roughly," Eli said. "Roughly is the best anyone can do."

His grandfather grunted, which could have meant anything, and picked up the black rock to weigh it in his hand before setting it back down exactly where it had been.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: To compare leases fairly, add the rent to every recurring cost the tenant pays, such as heat, electricity, water, internet and insurance, to get a total monthly cost.
story:
The driving school on Miller Road occupied a strip mall between a nail salon and a tax preparer, and its classroom smelled of burnt coffee and vinyl. Alexis sat in the back row with her permit in her pocket and two leases open on her phone, because Koralie had texted her at midnight with the news that she'd found them an apartment. "Six-fifty a month," Koralie whispered now, leaning across the aisle before Ms. Torres started the video on right-of-way. "The other one Josue's dad found is eight hundred. It's not even close."

Alexis had learned, somewhere in sixteen years of being impecunious, that when a deal was described as not even close, it was worth checking what was being compared. But she said nothing, because Ms. Torres dimmed the lights and started the video, and because part of her wanted the six-fifty to be true. She wanted it so much that during the break she let Koralie fill out the application on her phone while Josue read the lease over her shoulder, tracing the lines with one finger.

"Utilities aren't included," Josue said. He said it the way he said everything, flat, like reading a weather report. Koralie waved him off. "It's a hundred and fifty less, Josue. So we pay electric. Big deal."

"Electric, heat, water," Josue said. "Separate lines."

Alexis took the phone. She had a habit, when two things confused her, of trying to parametrize them, laying out the variables side by side the way Ms. Torres laid out the steps of a three-point turn: where you start, what you check, where you end. On a napkin from the coffee counter she wrote two columns. Under the six-fifty apartment she began listing everything the tenant paid every month, not just the rent: heat, electricity, water, internet, insurance. Under the eight hundred she listed the same things, where the second lease said they were included or billed flat.

Ms. Torres, collecting napkins for the second half of class, paused over her shoulder. "Homework?" she asked. Alexis covered it with her elbow. "Sort of," she said. "Life homework." Ms. Torres smiled and moved on, and Alexis kept adding, feeling the strange pleasure of watching something that had looked obvious turn into something that had to be worked out.

The columns filled. Rent plus heat, plus electricity, plus water, plus internet, plus insurance. She added each recurring cost the tenant paid to the rent in that column, line under line, until both columns ended in a total monthly cost. Then she looked at the two totals for a long moment before she said anything, because she wanted to be sure she was reading them right. "Koralie," she said finally. "The eight hundred place is cheaper."

"That's not how rent works," Koralie said.

"That's how living there works," Alexis said. "Rent's only the start. The six-fifty is six-fifty plus everything on this side of the napkin, every month, forever. The eight hundred is eight hundred and almost nothing else. Rent was a confounder, Koralie. It was hiding the rest." Josue took the napkin and checked her arithmetic twice, which was the closest he came to a compliment. Koralie stared at the columns, then at the application on her screen, then back at the columns, and Alexis watched her friend's certainty rearrange itself, slowly, the way furniture moves in a dark room.

"Okay," Koralie said. "Okay. The eight hundred place. I'll call about a viewing at lunch." She was already dialing, already apologizing to Josue's dad by voicemail, and Alexis sat back with the feeling of having solved something real, a problem with a method, a method she could use again on anything, on insurance quotes, on phone plans, on the whole sneaky architecture of fine print. She was so pleased with the napkin that she smoothed it flat and folded it into her binder like a document of state.

After class, her hour behind the wheel came up. Ms. Torres rode shotgun with the clipboard, and Alexis executed a three-point turn so clean that even Josue, waiting on the curb, raised an eyebrow. Then Ms. Torres flipped her clipboard page and mentioned, mildly, that the installment plan for the course had posted that morning, and that Alexis's mother's card on file had been declined. "You'll want to sort the balance before the next lesson," Ms. Torres said, "otherwise we pause the package." Alexis did the math without meaning to, the way she now always would: rent plus heat plus electricity plus water plus internet plus insurance, and then, at the bottom, the driving school. She looked at the folded napkin in her binder, at the neat columns that had proven so much, and out at the road where Koralie was still on the phone, saying, "Yes, we'll take the viewing, we can definitely afford it."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Heating and cooling bills change with the seasons, so averaging a full year of bills gives a truer monthly cost than a single month's bill.
story:
The two leases lay side by side on the kitchen table, and Zoe had promised Angelina she would have an answer by Sunday. Angelina had found the bigger place, the one on Delmore Street, and she wanted Zoe to sign with her in September, before someone else took it. The apartment Zoe liked better was Mr. Nasser's basement unit, two blocks from the college, cheaper by forty dollars a month on paper. She had spent the afternoon copying numbers into a notebook, and the numbers kept refusing to agree with her feelings.

"Everything's included at Delmore," Angelina said over the phone, her voice carrying the particular confidence of someone who had done half the research. "Water, heat, all of it. Mr. Nasser makes you pay your own utilities, so it's basically the same or worse." Zoe wrote this down, then looked at the page and felt the old suspicion her mother called cynicism and Zoe called arithmetic. "Included" was doing a lot of work in that sentence. The Delmore lease tacked on a hundred and twenty dollars a month for the utilities bundle, flat, all year.

Mr. Nasser had given her something else: a folder of the previous tenant's bills, twelve months of them, gas and electric combined. He had said only, "Read them in order, all twelve, not just the top one," and gone back upstairs. The top one was July, and it was twenty-eight dollars. Zoe sat with that number for a moment, imagining the summer, the basement's natural coolness, and how easy it would be to multiply twenty-eight by twelve and feel clever. She almost texted Angelina the total right then.

It was her grandmother, stirring soup at the stove behind her, who stopped her. "Your grandfather once budgeted off a June bill," her grandmother said without turning around. "By February we were eating rice." Zoe laughed, then didn't. She flipped to the January page. One hundred and eighty-six dollars. February was similar, and the shoulder months drifted between. A single month's bill, she understood slowly, was a photograph; a full year was a film. She added all twelve and divided, and the average came out to ninety-one dollars a month, which made Mr. Nasser's place a hundred and eleven dollars a month cheaper than Delmore, not more expensive.

She wanted it to be that simple. It wasn't, because Romain, who had lived in a basement suite his whole first year, came by that evening with his bike helmet still on and complicated everything. "Ask about the windows," he said. "Ours sweated all winter and the floor was like ice. Averaging the bills tells you the cost, not the comfort." He was right, and Zoe hated it a little, because she had been enjoying the clean feeling of a solved problem. The two ways of thinking sat in her notebook like rival witnesses: Angelina's flat-rate certainty, all safety and no information, and the twelve-month average, honest about cost but silent about everything else. Somewhere between them was the apartment as it would actually be lived in, and no formula would produce that.

She drafted a message to Angelina that began as a lecture and cut it. Instead she laid out both totals, the flat hundred and twenty and the averaged ninety-one, and wrote: "Delmore is more predictable. Nasser's is probably cheaper overall but I can't know exactly until we live through a winter in it." Her grandmother, reading over her shoulder in the way that was endemic to her and to grandmothers generally, offered the bromide that everything works out in the end, and Zoe didn't argue, though she privately believed that things worked out for people who had done the arithmetic first. What she could admit, even to herself, was that the averaging had changed less than she'd hoped. It adumbrated the real cost without revealing it; a cold year or a mild one could still bend the number either way, and no folder of someone else's bills would close that gap.

Angelina replied with a single question mark, then, ten minutes later: "Can we go see the basement on Saturday?" Zoe looked at the notebook, at the twelve bills lined up in their seasons, and then at the lease she hadn't signed. She texted Mr. Nasser to ask if Saturday morning was possible, and while she waited she opened the notebook to a fresh page and wrote, at the top, "Questions for the apartment: windows, thermostat, who shovels."

Mr. Nasser answered in his usual way, one word: "Come."

Zoe turned off the kitchen light and left both leases on the table, side by side, where her grandmother would see them in the morning and know she had not decided yet.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Under the US Help America Vote Act of 2002, a voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot, which counts only once officials confirm eligibility.
story:
The envelope had been sitting on the kitchen table since Tuesday, between the salt shaker and a stack of college brochures, and every time Sadie passed it she put a finger on its edge like testing a stove. Joe had texted twice that morning, a photo of his own ballot receipt with the caption "we're official," and Sahib had texted nothing, which was its own kind of message. She ate half a piece of toast, put her hair up, took it down, and slid the envelope into her jacket.

In the car she let her mother have the radio, and neither of them said the wordVote, though it filled the whole vehicle the way weather does. Sadie kept returning to November of junior year, to Ms. Kovalenko's classroom with its radiators that clanked like small artillery. They had been assigned to debate compulsory voting, and Sahib had taken the position that abstention was its own statement, principled even. Sadie had gone at him hard, harder than the assignment required, telling him he was dressing up laziness as philosophy, that staying home didn't extenuate anything, it just left the room emptier. Ms. Kovalenko had watched from her desk with her penurious little thermos of coffee, said nothing, and given them both the same grade.

The community hall smelled of floor wax and old coffee. A line of folding tables, a woman with a clipboard, a poster about sample ballots. Sadie gave her name, watched the woman's finger travel down a printed list, and travel down it again. Then a third time, slower, as though Sadie's name might have been hiding.

"You registered at the DMV in August?" the woman asked.

"August ninth."

The woman's mouth did something apologetic. "You're not in the book. Sometimes the paperwork doesn't come through in time." Behind Sadie, the line shifted its weight. "What you can do is cast a provisional ballot. It's under the Help America Vote Act. It counts once they confirm you're eligible." She was already reaching for a paper sleeve and a pen with a rubber band on it, so Sadie took them.

She filled in the ovals at a table by the window, and her hand was steadier than she expected, and then, sealing the envelope, less steady. The provisional part sat strangely in her mouth. Not a vote, exactly. A maybe-vote. She handed it over, got a slip with a phone number and a website, and walked out into the cold with her mother waiting at the curb, engine running.

That evening Sahib came over, ostensibly to return a library book he had borrowed in September, and stood in the kitchen holding it while she told them both the story. Joe was on speakerphone, propped against the fruit bowl.

"So it counts?" Joe asked.

"Once they confirm I was eligible to vote in the first place," Sadie said. "That's the whole deal. I looked it up when I got home. That's what a provisional ballot is." She turned her laptop around so the screen faced them, the government page with its plain headings, and felt obscurely proud of having researched it before explaining it, as though that were the part that proved something.

Sahib set the library book down and ran a thumb along its spine, not looking at anyone. "So you might have voted," he said. "Might."

"I voted in every way available to me," Sadie said. She heard Ms. Kovalenko's classroom in her own voice, that tone she'd used on Sahib junior year, and softened it. "Look, you don't have to think the system works to show up and make them count you. Both things can be true. You can think it's a mess and still put your name in the mess." She was thinking of him at seventeen, arguing beautifully for staying home, and she suspected now what she hadn't suspected then, that his argument had been less about principle than about the fear of casting something small into something enormous and watching it disappear.

Sahib was quiet for a moment. Then he pulled out his phone, and his thumb moved across it, and he held the screen up so she could see it: the county registrar's page, a registration form, the start of one, his legal name typed into the first field and nothing else filled in yet.

"Help me with the rest?" he said.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, including those who already have hypertension.
story:
Cameron found the cuff in his grandfather's bathroom cabinet, wedged between a bottle of antacids and a razor that had not been sharpened since the Clinton administration. The machine was a squat digital box with an arm sleeve and a button labeled START, and next to it, on a pad of graph paper, his grandfather had been keeping a record in pencil: numbers in two columns, morning and evening, going back months. Cameron had come for the weekend to help clean the gutters, but the pad interested him more than the gutters did, mostly because the numbers had been climbing all summer and his grandfather had said nothing about it.

"Grandad, what do these mean?" He carried the pad into the kitchen, where the old man sat with coffee and a crossword, looking, as he nearly always did, faintly saturnine, as though the crossword had personally wronged him.

"Top number's systolic, bottom's diastolic. The machine does the rest." His grandfather folded the paper over. "It's nothing. The doctor wants me to watch it, that's all."

The word hypertension appeared in his grandfather's discharge paperwork from June, which Cameron had been allowed to read only after promising not to fuss. He had looked it up on his phone in the bathroom, standing over the machine, and the phrases had stuck in his head the way the smell of his grandfather's house stuck to his jacket, pipe smoke and toast.

That afternoon Cameron took his own reading, mostly to test the machine. The cuff hissed and tightened until his arm went numb, then released, and the screen blinked out numbers that meant nothing to him. He resolved to fix that. He texted Nyla, who was doing a pharmacy tech program at the community college and answered all his medical questions with alarming enthusiasm.

She sent back a voice message, and he played it in the kitchen while his grandfather napped in the chair. Her voice came through tinny and bright against the hum of the refrigerator. "Okay, so, top number is the pressure when your heart beats, bottom is between beats. Higher than normal, that's hypertension, that's the word from the paperwork. And here's the part you actually want," and then, because a train passed wherever she was, he had to replay the last sentence twice. "Regular aerobic exercise, like brisk walking or cycling, most days, lowers blood pressure in lots of people. Even people who already have hypertension. It's not a maybe. It's most people. Write that down before you forget it."

He transcribed it onto the graph paper, word for word, in the margin beside the morning column, then sat back and looked at what he had. The walk thing was not a cure, and Nyla had not said it was. She had said it lowers it, in many people, which left a gap wide enough to drive a truck through, a gap shaped like whether it would work for his grandfather specifically. Cameron hated that gap. He also, having just finished a semester of statistics, respected it.

When his grandfather woke, Cameron put the machine on the table between them. "I took my own. I want to take yours."

"You want to poke at me like a medical student."

"Like a pharmacy tech, technically. Nyla's supervising by text." He wrapped the cuff around the thin arm, pressed START, and watched his grandfather watch the screen with the flat expression of a man waiting for a verdict. The number came up high, higher than any on the pad. Neither of them said anything for a moment. Then Cameron slid the graph paper across, with the transcribed sentence in the margin.

"I'm not asking you to become a cyclist," Cameron said. "I'm asking you to walk with me. Most days. There's a loop past Ms. Anderson's place, about a mile, and I saw her out pruning her roses yesterday so she'll absolutely comment on it, and honestly that could be our recompense for the boredom, she tells good stories."

His grandfather read the sentence twice. He tapped the margin with one finger. "Brisk," he said. "Not ambling."

"Brisk. Like you're late for something."

"Tomorrow, then," his grandfather said, and unfolded the crossword again, which Cameron understood to be the closest thing to an oath the man could offer.

The next evening they did the loop at a pace that made conversation come in short bursts, past Ms. Anderson's fence, past the drainage pond where two boys were failing to catch frogs. His grandfather did not huff, exactly, but breathed audibly, and when they finished he stood in the driveway with his hands on his hips. "Again Thursday," he said. Cameron marked it on the graph paper when they got inside, a W in the margin, and left the blood pressure machine on the table where they would both see it in the morning.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they do not depend on daily use.
story:
I wasn't nervous about the presentation, which is why I'd left preparing for it until Sunday night. Our health teacher had signed me up for the peer-education thing in September, back when volunteering still felt like a line on a college application and not an actual room with actual ninth graders in it. Monday morning I would stand in front of them and explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested at the clinic on Marsh Street. All of it. In eight minutes. Tyce had been assigned the same material for a different class and he'd already written his talk, which he kept mentioning, so I called him and Lynden over to my house to rehearse, mostly to prove I didn't need to rehearse.

They showed up at four with my mom's grocery-store pretzels and an obstreperous attitude, Tyce especially, drumming on my desk and claiming the whole unit was pointless because everyone learned this from the internet anyway. "That's exactly the problem," Lynden said. She was the only one of us who'd actually gone to the Marsh Street clinic last spring, for a sore throat she'd been convinced was something worse, and she'd come home with a canvas bag of pamphlets she now spread across my bed like tarot cards. "The internet doesn't check on you afterward."

I compartmentalized, is what I did. The part of me that was fine with the presentation went in one box and the part that kept imagining thirty fourteen-year-olds staring at me went in another, and I started my run-through. Consent first. I'd written it out plainly: consent has to be freely given, informed, and revocable, and a person can change their mind at any point, and being silent isn't the same as saying yes. Saying it out loud in my own bedroom, with the radiator ticking and the February light going gray at the window, made it sound both simpler and heavier than it had on the page.

Then contraception, and that was where I got sloppy. "The pill, the IUD, the implant, the shot, they're all in the same ballpark," I said, shuffling my cards. "Like high nineties percent effective."

Tyce stopped drumming. Lynden picked up a pamphlet and read it, then read it again, the paper crackling under her thumb. "That's not what it says. I asked the nurse about this when I was there, because I asked her about everything, I made her rate every method like a food critic." She held the pamphlet toward me. "Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they don't depend on daily use." She tapped the margin. "The pill works about as well in theory, but you have to take it every single day, and people forget, so in real life it fails more."

"So it's not about which one is stronger," I said slowly. "It's about which one doesn't rely on you remembering." That was the thing I'd been missing, the reason the clinic's whole wall chart ranked methods the way it did. I felt stupid, and then less stupid, because at least I'd found out on a Sunday with two friends instead of on a Monday in front of a room.

The testing part was easier to say than I expected, maybe because Lynden had walked me through her own visit: how you could walk in without an appointment, how everything was confidential, how the forms took ten minutes and the nurse didn't lecture you, how results came by phone or a secure message. I said all of that out loud and Tyce actually wrote some of it down, which he'd deny later. He kept saying the ninth graders wouldn't listen, that the zeitgeist, as he put it, was that nobody listened to anyone older than twenty, and Lynden kept saying that hadn't stopped the nurse from being heard, that a person with facts and no smirk could get through to almost anybody.

We ordered pizza and ran it twice more, and the second time I got through all eight minutes without once looking at the cards, which I attributed to my natural composure and not at all to the fact that my hands were shaking so hard I'd put them in my pockets. Lynden stayed after Tyce left, re-folding the pamphlets into their bag. "You know you're going to get a question you can't answer," she said. "Some kid's going to ask something the pamphlets don't cover."

"I'll say I don't know and find out," I said.

She zipped the bag shut and looked at me for a long second, like she was deciding whether to believe me, and then she said, "That's the right answer," and put her coat on.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, US workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of $899, compared with $708 for those without one.
story:
Blake wore the gown zipped only to mid-chest because the June air was already thick at nine in the morning, and because he had decided, on the walk from the parking lot, that dignity was negotiable and ventilation was not. The folding chairs had been set up on the football field in rows that curved like a phylogeny chart Mr. Clarke-Williams had shown them in biology, every seat a branch off some common ancestor of folding chairs, and Blake had laughed at that thought alone, which made Tatum, seated to his left, lean over and ask if he was already crying.

"Not yet," Blake said. "Give the principal ten minutes."

The ceremony ran long. A student speaker quoted a dead poet, the choir recovered from a key change the way a person recuperates from a bad flu, slowly and with visible effort, and Mr. Clarke-Williams read names at a pace that suggested he understood exactly how hot the black gowns were. When he reached Blake's name, Blake crossed the stage, shook the hand, took the folder with the certificate inside, and heard his father whistle from somewhere in the stands, two short bursts, the same whistle he used when Blake mowed the lawn in a single pass.

Afterward there were sandwiches under a tent by the concession stand. His uncle had driven four hours and arrived with a cooler and an opinion, which was his usual luggage. He cornered Blake near the lemonade.

"You know what that thing is worth?" his uncle said, nodding at the folder Blake still carried. "In 2023, US workers twenty-five and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of eight hundred ninety-nine dollars. Without one, seven hundred and eight. I looked it up before I came. That's a hundred ninety-one dollars a week."

Blake did the math on a napkin while Tatum, standing nearby with her own folder tucked under her arm like a clipboard, watched him do it. Around ten thousand a year, he wrote, and then, under it, roughly half a million over a working life, and then he crossed out the last figure because he suspected it was too neat, the kind of number people invented to make a point land harder.

His father came over with a paper plate of potato salad and heard the last part. "You can't measure a thing like that in dollars," his father said.

"You can," his uncle said. "Bureau of Labor Statistics does it all the time."

"I mean you shouldn't."

Blake stood between them with the napkin in his hand. His father had left school at seventeen and run a two-truck landscaping business for twenty years, and he said, often, that he had never once been asked for a diploma, only for whether he could show up at six. His uncle worked in insurance and said, just as often, that the world paid more politely to people with the right paper. Both of them were right about their own lives, which Blake had begun to suspect was the whole problem with advice.

"That's the median," Blake said, mostly to the napkin. "Half the people with diplomas make less than that."

His uncle opened his mouth, then closed it, then took some potato salad off his father's plate, which was apparently the family gesture for conceding a point without saying so.

Audrey-Anne found them there and took a photo of Blake between the two men, one hand still holding the napkin with the arithmetic on it. She promised to send it to everyone and then photographed the napkin too, "for the archive," she said, which was a joke whose full meaning Blake did not get and decided not to chase. She was going to a state school in the fall to study nursing. Tatum was going into a machinist apprenticeship, no degree required, and had said, that morning, that she planned to outearn all of them by thirty.

Blake had spent the spring caught between two ways of talking about his future. His mother's side of the family spoke in doors opening, in options, in the phenotypic advantages of a good transcript, visible to employers like a trait that had been selected for. His father spoke in hours and invoices and the specific pleasure of a customer who paid on time. Neither language translated fully into the other. The statistics his uncle quoted were real, Blake assumed, and still they described a million people at once, none of whom was him. He did not know yet whether he would finish college or need to or want to, and he noticed that saying so, even silently, felt less like weakness than it had in April.

Under the tent, his uncle told a story about a man he had worked with who faked his credentials for eleven years and was caught because he could not operate the coffee machine on the executive floor. His father said the coffee machine was the credential now, and both of them laughed, and Tatum said she would put that on her shop wall.

The chairs were being stacked. The field, emptied of its rows, went back to being just grass with yard lines on it. Blake folded the napkin along the crease his arithmetic had made and put it in the pocket of the gown, which he was not giving back until someone made him.

"Still hot?" Tatum asked.

"Still hot," Blake said, and pulled the zipper the rest of the way down.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
story:
The application had asked for her availability and her emergency contact and whether she had reliable transportation, and Rosalie had answered everything honestly except the question about experience, where she had written "cashiering at my mom's pharmacy, informal," which was technically true and practically nothing. Now she stood at the counter of the coffee shop on Fenwick Street waiting for Mr. Sato, who owned it, to come back from the storeroom. The morning light came through the front windows in wide yellow bands across the tile floor, and the espresso machine hissed behind her in a way that sounded like something alive being kept in a cabinet.

"You can start Saturday," Mr. Sato said, reappearing with a crate of cups balanced on one hip. "Training shift. Whitney usually trains the new people."

"Whitney from my school?" Rosalie asked. "Whitney Adair?"

"The same one. She's good with the machine." He set the crate down and rubbed his shoulder. "There's a deli case in the back now, too. Sandwiches, cold cuts. It's been good business. The slicer came last month."

Rosalie had eaten at the shop twice before, once with her mother and once alone, and both times she had noticed the pastry case but not the deli case, which she now saw along the far wall, glass-fronted, with a stainless steel machine beside it whose blade was half the size of a dinner plate. She felt an odd pull looking at it, half attraction and half warning, the way she felt about the whole job. She wanted the money, plainly and without embarrassment. She wanted it for the train pass and the deposit on a dorm her financial aid wouldn't cover, and she had decided that wanting money plainly was more respectable than pretending she wanted experience.

Saturday came warm and gray. Whitney tied an apron on Rosalie from behind like a nurse adjusting a hospital gown, then walked her through the register, the grinder, the timer for the drip coffee that had to be dumped every two hours regardless of whether it smelled fine. Whitney was brisk and funny and kept up a running commentary on the regulars, the man who ordered a large even though he complained large was too much, the woman who paid in quarters. At eleven the lunch crowd started, and Mr. Sato called from the back that he needed turkey cut thin and roast beef cut thick, because a catering order had come in that he hadn't mentioned to anyone until now.

"I'll do the turkey," Whitney said, then stopped, because the phone was ringing and Mr. Sato was waving her toward it, and a man in a paint-splattered jacket was waiting at the counter, and the whole shop seemed to lean forward on its hinges. "Rosalie, can you do the slicer? Thin on the turkey, thick on the roast beef. It's easy, you just set the dial."

Rosalie looked at the dial. It was a small numbered wheel on the side of the machine, and the blade had a guard, and the turkey was already out of the case in a waxed paper sleeve. It did look easy. She put her hand on the handle and then took it off again, because something Olivier had said in the school library in March had surfaced without warning, the way things she had half-listened to always did, months later, at the worst possible moment. He had been reading a forum thread about his older brother's grocery job, and he had read one line aloud, offhand, testing it on her: under US federal child labor rules, workers under eighteen may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant. She had said something dismissive at the time. She couldn't remember what.

"I can't," she said. "I'm eighteen, but I'm not. I mean I am eighteen, I just, I'm not sure I can."

Whitney put her hand over the phone receiver. "What?"

"I'm not eighteen," Rosalie said, and the words came out slower than she wanted them to. "My birthday's in August. I turn eighteen before college, I just, I'm still seventeen now." She hadn't lied on the application; it had asked her age in years and she had answered, and only in the last second had she thought about how the answer was already changing, how in four months it would be a different answer to the same person.

Whitney looked at her for a long moment. The espresso machine hissed. The man in the paint-splattered jacket coughed. Then Whitney laughed, short and relieved. "God. For a second I thought you were going to say the machine was haunted." She put the receiver back to her ear, said something into it, and hung up. "It's fine, I'll do it. Do the register, do the sandwiches, stay off the slicer until August. Mr. Sato won't care, he just forgets to think about it. He forgets I'm not allowed to either until June."

"Until June?" Rosalie said.

"I'm seventeen too. That's the whole reason he has to do the slicing himself half the time, which he hates, so he tends to forget." Whitney pulled on a glove. "Honestly, it's a quagmire back there, which is probably why his attitude about it is so equivocal. Don't ask him about the child labor poster unless you have an hour."

Rosalie took the paint-splattered man's order, made his drink, watched the foam settle. She had spent months thinking about the job as one thing, money shaped like an apron and a Sunday shift, and it turned out to be made of smaller decisions, each with its own edge. She had almost said yes.
