That was the part that sat strangely with her, not that the rule existed but that she had reached for the handle before remembering it, and that if Olivier hadn't been bored in the library in March she might have found out some other way, or not. She wasn't sure whether she had done something good or only something lucky, and she could feel the two of them sitting side by side in her, refusing to merge.

"Turkey's done," Whitney called, slicing with an ease that made the forbiddenness of it look theoretical. "Wrap it and come taste one of these, they're actually incredible."

Rosalie wrapped the turkey, folding the paper under like her mother did at the pharmacy, and came around the counter, and took the triangle of bread Whitney held out, still warm where the cheese had melted.

"Now tell me everything about the dorm situation," Whitney said. "And don't demur, because I have opinions about roommates and I need material."

"Well," Rosalie said, chewing, "my mother thinks I should live at home the first year."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The law of conservation of mass means the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants in a closed system.
story:
The practice problem had been sitting in front of Andrew for eleven minutes: 25.0 grams of zinc reacting with hydrochloric acid, how many moles of hydrogen gas form. He knew the first step, look up the molar mass of zinc, 65.38 grams per mole, and he knew the last step, and it was the middle he couldn't see across. On the lab bench beside him, Dustin was building a tower out of his calculator, two pens and an eraser, which suggested Dustin had finished or had never started.

"You're supposed to divide first," Eloic said, leaning over from the next stool without being invited. "Mass by molar mass. That's the whole trick."

"Thanks," Andrew said, and did not divide, because being told the trick and seeing the trick were, in his experience, different subjects entirely. He wrote 25.0 and then wrote nothing under it.

Mr. Sultani circulated with his hands behind his back, the way he did when he wanted everyone to feel watched in a gentle, vaguely feudal manner. He paused at Andrew's page. "You did this in the demo last week," he said. "The sealed bag."

The flashback arrived before Andrew could stop it, which was how his memory usually worked. Last Tuesday, the demonstration table at the front, a zip bag on the balance with vinegar and baking soda weighed separately and then together, 84.2 grams. Mr. Sultani had mixed them inside the sealed bag, the fizzing, the bag going taut like a small pillow, everyone waiting for the number to be different, and the balance still reading 84.2. Dustin, out loud, to nobody: "That's it?" Eloic had said "the law of conservation of mass," flatly, as if reciting a password, and Mr. Sultani had only nodded and moved on to washing out the beaker, leaving the class to sit with the number.

In the present, Andrew looked at his zinc problem again. The gas would escape if you did it in an open beaker, that was the thing, the gas was part of the products, it counted even when you couldn't see it leave. And the zinc going into the reaction was the thing you had, 25.0 grams of it, and if you wanted to know how much of it there actually was, in the units the equation spoke, you divided by how heavy each unit was. Molar mass wasn't a wall between the steps. It was a conversion, the same mass, counted in a different currency.

He divided 25.0 by 65.38 and got 0.382 moles of zinc. The balanced equation said one mole of zinc produced one mole of hydrogen gas. He wrote 0.382 moles H2 and then, feeling something inchoate take shape, a suspicion that he'd been treating the middle of problems as magic rather than as accounting, he checked it against the conservation idea: the atoms hadn't vanished, they had only been rearranged, so the counting before and the counting after had to agree. The moles were just bookkeeping for the atoms.

"Wait," Eloic said, reading upside down. "You didn't use the trick."

"I used it. I just used it late."

Dustin's tower collapsed, one pen rolling off the bench and onto the floor, where nobody retrieved it. "Can one of you contextualize this for me," he said, "because I have been staring at the word stoichiometry for ten minutes and it has stopped looking like a word."

"It means the ratios," Eloic said. "How much of this makes how much of that."

"Which is the whole middle of the problem," Andrew said, and rotated his notebook so Dustin could see the layout: grams on the left, divided through, moles on the right, the equation above like a recipe. He was aware, in a way he didn't entirely trust yet, that he had assembled this from two places, the demo's stubborn number and Eloic's flat password of a phrase, and that neither source had explained anything at the time. Mr. Sultani had refused to, actually, which Andrew was beginning to suspect had been the point. Though he couldn't be sure whether that was pedagogy or laziness, and he filed the question under unresolved.

Mr. Sultani drifted back, looked at the 0.382, and raised one eyebrow a distance that could have meant anything. "Try it with 40.0 grams," he said, and moved on.

Andrew set up the new problem, dividing 40.0 by 65.38, and the number that came out, 0.612, pleased him more than an answer should. Dustin leaned over with his calculator finally in hand, and Eloic, still reading upside down, said, "You're going to want to show the conversion."

"Show me yours first," Andrew said, and covered his page with his elbow.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Many food banks cannot accept home-cooked or opened food, because they cannot check how it was prepared or stored.
story:
The food bank had taken over the library's meeting room for the third Saturday of the month, and by ten past nine the folding tables were already lined with cans and boxed pasta, sorted by a volunteer named Reagan, who had done this many times before and moved with the certainty of someone who had. Christopher stood near the door with a clipboard, which was the job Mr. MacLeod had given him, checking people in and pointing them toward the donation table. He had signed up because his mother had mentioned it once, lightly, over dinner, that it would look good on applications, and because after she said it he could not stop hearing the sentence, though he was not sure whether that was a reason to go or a reason not to.

Mr. MacLeod, the librarian, wanted the whole morning to run smoothly. He had negotiated for weeks with the county to let the food bank use the room, and he kept drifting over from the circulation desk to straighten the sign-in sheets and adjust the banner someone had taped slightly crooked above the door. "First impressions," he said to Christopher, tapping the banner. "People decide in a moment whether a place is for them."

Zachary arrived at half past nine, an hour late, carrying a bakery box with both hands like something fragile. He had been at Christopher's school since seventh grade, and lately everything he did had the shape of a college application. "Forty hours of service," he said, setting the box down. "That's the number I need before December. Is this where they count them?"

Reagan looked up from the pasta. "There's a sheet you sign at the end. Don't lose it."

The box, when Christopher opened it, held a lasagna, still warm through the cardboard. Zachary's grandmother had made it, he explained, because he had told her he was volunteering at a food bank and she had said, in the way of grandmothers, that no one should have to eat from a can when there was a kitchen in the world. He was proud of it. He kept his hand on the lid.

"We should check," Christopher said, because he had read the volunteer guidelines in the car that morning, mostly the first page, which had been about punctuality and closed-toe shoes, and he remembered something further down that he had skimmed.

Reagan came over, wiping her hands on her jeans, and lifted the lid a fraction. Steam curled up, and the cheese had browned in little blisters along the edge. "We can't take this," she said. Not unkindly, but plainly. "Food banks can't accept home-cooked food or anything opened. There's no way for us to check how it was prepared or stored."

Zachary stood very still. "It's lasagna," he said, as if the problem were identification.

"I know it's lasagna. It smells incredible."

Christopher had spent the fall in an ethics seminar his school offered, where the teacher liked to historicize every argument, tracing each position back to some older one, as if an idea were illegitimate unless you could name its parents. He had enjoyed it more than he admitted. There was a pleasure in seeing that a rule was not natural, that someone had made it, at some table, for some reason. But standing between the warm box and the folding tables, he found the pleasure had gone thin. The rule Reagan had recited was made-up, historically, by people, and it was also the only thing standing between a stranger's stomach and a kitchen nobody had inspected. Both of those were true at once.

"Can she take it to a shelter?" Christopher asked. "Somewhere it gets eaten right away?"

"Some do hot meals," Reagan said. "You'd have to call around." She turned back to her cans, because the morning was moving and there was a line forming near the tables.

The line. That was the part Christopher had not pictured when he signed up. A man in a windbreaker with two young kids, a woman he recognized vaguely from the hardware store, an older man who greeted Mr. MacLeod by name and was greeted back without any change in the librarian's voice, which seemed, in its steadiness, like a kindness. Nobody's situation was announced. They took what they took and said thank you, or said nothing, and Christopher marked their visits on the clipboard with a check, and the checks looked exactly the same.

Zachary took the box back from the table and stood holding it in the doorway between the meeting room and the stacks, where the tall windows let down their quiet light onto the biography section. "Forty hours," he said again, but quieter, as if testing whether the sentence still held the same weight. Christopher thought of telling him that the hours would count regardless, that the lasagna had never been part of the math, and then thought better of it, because that was not entirely true either. Zachary's grandmother had made it out of something the clipboard could not record, and the food bank could not accept it, and both of those facts would sit side by side in the doorway for as long as Zachary stood there.

Mr. MacLeod appeared with a roll of tape and rehung the banner himself, level this time. He surveyed the room, the line, the sorted shelves, the ancillary table by the far wall where diapers and soap were kept, things people forgot food banks needed. "Good turnout," he said, mostly to himself.

Christopher went to find the phone number for the shelter downtown, and copied it onto a slip of paper, and handed it to Zachary, who folded it into his pocket without looking at it. "Tell her it fed somebody either way," Christopher said. Zachary nodded slowly, tucked the box under one arm, and pushed out through the double doors into the parking lot, where he stood for a moment beside his car, deciding.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2010 study claimed 'power poses' raised testosterone and lowered cortisol, but a larger 2015 replication found no such hormonal effect, though people still reported feeling more powerful.
story:
Angelina's mother had taped the job listing to the refrigerator weeks ago, a pithy paragraph advertising a weekend counter position at the cheese shop two streets over, and every morning it had watched her eat her toast until she finally circled it in green marker and called the number. The owner wanted to interview her on Saturday, on video, because he was away at a food fair. That gave her four days to become a person who could look someone in the eye and answer questions without her voice thinning out like wet paper.

On Wednesday evening, Louka came over with a bag of sour candies and a legal pad. "We're doing this properly," Louka said, arranging the kitchen chairs so that one faced the window, where the afternoon light could burnish Angelina's face into something less like a hostage recording. "Question one. Tell me about yourself."

Angelina began with her grade average, then her ability to arrive places on time, then trailed into a description of her paper route from sixth grade, which she had quit. Louka let her finish, then shook her head. "You looked at the table the entire time. There's a table between you in this scenario? There isn't even a table."

Jasmin arrived halfway through, having read something on the bus. "Okay, so there's this thing," she said, pulling out her phone. "You stand like a superhero before the interview. Feet apart, hands on hips. A 2010 study claimed power poses raised testosterone and lowered cortisol." She squinted at the screen. "Cortisol, that's the stress one. But then a larger study in 2015 tried to replicate it and found no such hormonal effect." She looked up. "People still reported feeling more powerful, though. So it might be all in your head."

"Then it's fake," Louka said.

"It's not fake if it works," Jasmin said. "It's just fake hormones."

They tried it in the bathroom, the only room with a full-length mirror, all three of them packed in among the towels, standing with their hands on their hips like a low-budget crime-fighting team. Angelina held the pose for two minutes and felt, honestly, a little ridiculous, and also a little taller. She could not tell whether anything in her blood had changed, and she suspected that was the whole problem with the idea. The 2015 study had measured the blood, and the blood had said nothing happened, but the people had still said they felt more powerful, and she did not know which of those mattered more for a cheese shop interview, or for anything.

She thought about it again on Thursday while making her mother's coffee, standing at the counter with her hands on her hips, waiting for the kettle. Maybe the pose was a way of practicing the posture of confidence until the posture stopped being a costume. Or maybe it was just a small lie she was telling her own body, and the honest thing was to accept being nervous. Her mother, watching from the doorway, said, "You look like you're about to give me a raise." Angelina laughed, and decided, for the moment, that she would do the pose and also be nervous, both at once, and that neither cancelled the other out. That was as far as she could honestly get.

Saturday morning she set the laptop on a stack of cookbooks so the camera sat at eye level, tested the light, and locked the bathroom door for two minutes of superhero standing before the call. When the owner's face filled the screen, a heavy man with flour on his apron who introduced himself as a devoted epicure and began describing the shop's forty-one cheeses with visible joy, Angelina answered the first question while looking directly into the little green dot above the screen rather than at his face. Her voice held. When he asked about weaknesses, she said she was sometimes too quiet with strangers, and that she was working on it, which happened to be true, and he nodded as though this were a reasonable thing for a seventeen-year-old to be doing with herself.

At the end, he said he would call by Tuesday, and Angelina closed the laptop and stood in the middle of the kitchen, hands drifting toward her hips without her deciding it. Her mother came in from the garden and asked how it went.

"I don't know yet," Angelina said. "But I looked him in the eye the whole time."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Islamic law, ijtihad is the independent reasoning a qualified scholar uses to apply the Quran and hadith to questions the texts do not directly answer.
story:
Keira spread the photocopies across the kitchen table and weighted the curling edges with mugs. The assignment sheet sat at the top: choose a rule from a sacred text, argue in a formal debate whether it still applies, and cite only the text itself. Ms. Diallo had underlined the last clause twice.

Riba, the prohibition on interest, was the rule her group had drawn by lottery. Asher had wanted euthanasia and Raphael had argued for dietary laws, but the folded paper Keira picked said riba, and so riba it was. She had spent the evening at the dining table while her mother cooked, exhuming verse after verse from the Quran on her laptop, copying down Surah Al-Baqarah 2:275, where trade is permitted and interest is condemned, and the hadith about the exchange of gold for gold, like for like, hand to hand.

"Your dinner's getting cold," her mother said.

"In a minute." She wrote the verse out on an index card, then turned the card over and stared at the blank side. That was the side for the modern world, and the modern world had a problem: her debate was against the proposition that the rule still applies, and every argument she had prepared was about payday loans and credit card debt, things the text never mentioned. Ms. Diallo would knock points off for evidence outside the source. The room had gone quiet enough that she could hear the extractor fan.

Asher arrived at eight with his laptop under his arm and a bag of burnt popcorn. He was on the opposing side, arguing the rule still applied, and they had agreed to run a practice round in Keira's kitchen, which their coach thought was a kind of detente and which they both understood was a way to size each other up.

"Opening statement," Asher said, standing at the end of the table as if it were a podium. "The prohibition on riba is stated in the text without exception. Trade is permitted, interest is forbidden. There is no verse that says, except in the case of mortgages."

"That's not an argument, that's a reading," Keira said. "A profligate reading, actually. You're stretching seven words across fourteen centuries and pretending nothing has changed." She heard her own voice get sharper than she meant it to.

"It's the text itself. That's the whole assignment."

"Then the assignment is broken." She pushed the laptop toward him. On the screen was a page she had found at midnight, a forum for students of Islamic jurisprudence, where a teenager had asked how scholars rule on things like online banking that did not exist in the texts. She scrolled down to the reply. "Read the third answer."

Asher read it, and his mouth moved slightly, the way it did when he was memorizing. The reply described ijtihad, the independent reasoning a qualified scholar uses to apply the Quran and hadith to questions the texts do not directly answer. The answerer gave an example: whether a car lease counts as a sale or a loan, decided by reasoning from the principles of both.

"That helps you more than it helps me," Asher said finally.

"How?"

"Because you can argue that a rule applied through ijtihad is not the same rule anymore. It's been reasoned into a new shape. The text's version is fourteen centuries old. The living version is whatever a scholar says it is today."

Keira took the laptop back and read the passage a second time. It did not say that. It said the opposite, she thought, or something adjacent to the opposite: that the reasoning drew its authority from the text, the way a root draws from soil. Two readings of one paragraph, both defensible, and she sat with the discomfort of holding both at once.

"Or," she said slowly, "it helps you. Ijtihad means the rule reaches things the text never touched, which means it applies more now, not less. It applies to my debit card."

"It can't be both."

"It has to be both. That's what it is." She pulled a fresh index card toward her and wrote two columns, one for each side of the room she might argue from, and found she could fill both without lying in either. The burnt popcorn smell had reached the table. Her mother set a plate of food beside the cards and turned off the extractor fan, and the kitchen went silent except for Asher, who reached over and turned the card so he could read her handwriting.

"You're going to argue both sides," he said.

"I'm going to argue the honest one," Keira said, and crossed out the column she had labeled in favor, then uncrossed it.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Chinese red-envelope gifts avoid amounts containing the number four, because the word for 'four' sounds like the word for 'death'.
story:
The cultural center smelled like star anise and fried dough, and Seth stood near the door holding a stack of red envelopes his mother had pressed into his hands before disappearing into the crowd. His job was simple: find the younger cousins at the lunar new year banquet, hand each one an envelope, and make sure his brother did not eat his body weight in dumplings. The problem was the envelopes were empty. His mother had given him a fold of twenties and told him to fill them himself, which felt like being handed a live wire with instructions to be careful.

He found a table near the stage, where the lion dance would start in an hour, and began counting money into the first envelope. Twenty for one cousin, twenty for the next. His youngest cousin, seven and missing a front tooth, slid onto the bench beside him and started building his own pile with a fistful of bills he had gotten from their grandfather.

"I'm putting in forty," the cousin announced, arranging two twenties with the ceremony of a bank teller. "Forty is the biggest number I know how to count by twenties."

Seth reached over and caught his wrist, not because he knew anything but because something in the way a woman at the next table had glanced over made him pause. "Hold on. Wait a second."

Camila from his chemistry class appeared at his elbow, holding a cup of tea and a paper plate of sesame balls. "You're doing it wrong," she said, in the tone she used when someone mislabeled a beaker.

"Doing what wrong?"

"That. Forty dollars." She set her plate down. "My grandma would faint. You can't give amounts with a four in them. In Chinese, the word for four sounds like the word for death."

Seth looked at the two twenties in his cousin's small hands. "Sounds like it? Exactly, or sort of?"

"Sort of close enough that nobody does it. My aunt once got a gift of four of something and she still talks about it." Camila popped a sesame ball into her mouth. "Give eight, or six. Eight's the lucky one."

His cousin, who had been listening with the gravity of someone being told the floor was lava, began trying to extract one twenty and replace it with a ten, which would have made thirty, which apparently solved nothing, since four was hiding inside it. Seth watched him try to reason through the arithmetic and felt something shift in his own head, the way two separate pages of notes sometimes coagulate into one idea worth keeping. He had spent all of last semester in Mr. Paquette's advisory hour arguing that traditions were just arbitrary rules people forgot the reasons for, and Mr. Paquette had leaned back in his chair and said, "Arbitrary to whom?" Seth had not had an answer then and did not have one now, sitting here with death hiding inside a number.

He took out his phone and checked, because he wanted the shape of it. In Mandarin, the sounds were close, cousins of each other, not identical. So it was not law, it was resemblance. It reminded him of chemistry, the way carbon was the same element whether it was graphite in a pencil or a diamond in a ring, an allotrope, one thing wearing different forms. The number four and the number eight were just numbers; the meaning was something people built around them. But his cousin was still sitting there refusing to touch the twenties, and that refusal was real too. Mr. Paquette had asked, "Arbitrary to whom?" and maybe that was the whole answer: not arbitrary to the grandmother, not arbitrary to the aunt who still talked about it, and therefore not arbitrary in any way that mattered.

"Fine," Seth said. He traded his cousin two tens and a five back for one twenty, and wrote twenty-five on the little gold sticker his mother had included for sealing the envelopes. He did the rest by feel, twenty for each cousin, keeping every amount clear of the number Camila had flagged, and he noticed that he was not doing it out of belief, exactly, but out of something adjacent to belief, a kind of courtesy toward a system he could see the edges of without standing inside it. Was that respect, or was it just hedging? He genuinely did not know, and the not knowing did not feel like failure. It felt like the first week of a language class, when you could recognize words without producing them yet.

The drums started up for the lion dance, and the crowd moved toward the stage like water finding a channel. His cousin grabbed his sleeve and pulled, the envelope with twenty-five dollars in it already forgotten, attention coagulated entirely on the enormous painted head bobbing through the doors. Somewhere in the noise, Seth thought he saw a strain of the old worry pass over the face of a grandmother near the stage, the virulent certainty that one wrong number could undo a whole year's luck, and he understood even that, even if he could not share it.

Camila tugged his other sleeve. "You're staring," she said. "Come on, they're throwing lettuce."

He let himself be pulled forward, one envelope still warm in his jacket pocket, and caught the paper-wrapped money that rained down when the lion shook its head.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: The 'file drawer problem', a term coined by psychologist Robert Rosenthal in 1979, describes studies with null results going unpublished, which makes the published record look more positive than the evidence.
story:
Grayson spread the two photocopies across the library table like a hand of cards he didn't want to play. Both articles asked the same question, whether after-school music programs improved reading scores in middle school, and both concluded that they did. His assignment, printed in Ms. Zhang's careful hand at the top of the instruction sheet, was to write a critical review comparing them, which sounded simple until he actually read them. The first study tracked four hundred students in Ohio. The second was smaller, messier, set in Toronto, and its authors apologized for their sample in the third paragraph. He had been sitting in the third-floor reading room for an hour, and so far his notes said, in their entirety: "They agree."

"You look like someone stole your pencil," said Melinda, dropping into the chair across from him with a stack of books she had no intention of reading. She was supposed to be researching her own paper on urban renewal, but her idea of research involved finding one source and declaring victory.

"They both say music helps," Grayson said. "I'm supposed to compare them, but there's nothing to compare. It's like being asked to critique two people for saying the sky is blue."

Melinda leaned over and flipped the Ohio article around to face her. "So say they're both right and go get food."

"That's not a critical review. That's a summary." He heard how prissy it sounded and kept going anyway, because it was true. Ms. Zhang had written in the margin of his last draft, "Where are you in this?" and the question had lodged in him like a splinter he couldn't reach. He wanted to find it and pull it out.

He spent the next forty minutes in the stacks instead, hunting through the journals Ms. Zhang had left on the reserve shelf, and it was there, standing between the metal shelves under a buzzing fluorescent tube, that he found the third article. Same question, same kind of study, a school district in Manchester. Except this one had found nothing at all. No improvement in reading scores, none, the music students and the non-music students separated by a difference so small the authors called it indistinguishable from chance. Grayson read the abstract twice. Then he looked at the date. It had been published in a small regional journal, the kind so obscure it seemed practically obsolescent, its spine cracked and its pages already yellowing, while the two positive studies sat in glossy, heavily cited flagship journals. He carried all three back to the table with the feeling of someone who has picked up a coin in the street and can't decide if it's luck or a trap.

"Okay," he said to Melinda, laying the Manchester article beside the others. "What if every study I found was never a fair sample? What if there were ten more like this one that nobody ever printed?"

Melinda frowned at him. "Why wouldn't they print them?"

"That's the thing. The stuff that works gets published. The stuff that doesn't just sits in somebody's drawer." He was working it out as he said it, the way a key finds a lock. "It's called the file drawer problem. I think I read that somewhere." He hadn't; he was remembering it now, half a page in one of the articles he'd skimmed, something a psychologist named Robert Rosenthal had named in 1979. Studies with null results going unpublished, so the whole published record ends up looking more positive than the evidence actually is. He went back through the Ohio article and there it was, a single sentence in the limitations section, almost apologetic, like the authors were checking a box.

He texted Sophie, the one person he knew who would care. She had written a paper the previous spring in which every single source supported her thesis, all nine of them, and she had been proud of it until Ms. Zhang asked, in front of the whole class, what the nine sources she couldn't find might have said. "Question," he typed. "For your paper last year. When every article you found agreed with you, did that ever seem weird? Because I've got two studies saying music helps reading and one saying it does nothing, and the one that says nothing was almost impossible to find. Wondering if the pattern is the story, not any single study." Her reply came while he was watching the screen. "That's actually horrifying. I thought I had done good work. I had just found the papers that got to exist." Then, a minute later: "Okay. I'm redoing part of it. Ms. Zhang is going to think I lost my mind."

Grayson sat with that for a moment. He had changed her mind, or the articles had, or Robert Rosenthal had, forty years before either of them was born, and the thought transfigured the whole afternoon for him: the library was not a warehouse of answers but a survivors' record, and reading it honestly meant keeping the missing in view. He picked up his pen. At the top of a fresh page he wrote, "A review of two studies must ask not only what they found, but what we would be reading if the findings had been different." Under it he began drafting the comparison, the Ohio sample against the Toronto one, the confident tone against the apologetic one, both of them now looking slightly less like the sky being blue and slightly more like two people who had won a lottery and mistaken themselves for the whole population of players.

Melinda, watching him write, pulled her urban renewal stack closer and opened the top book with visible reluctance. "If every source says the highway was good for the city," she said slowly, "that's suspicious too, right?"

"That's the review," Grayson said, and slid the Manchester article across the table to her, its yellowed pages still warm from the photocopier upstairs.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Many driving courses teach keeping at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead, and a longer gap in rain, snow or darkness.
story:
The washing machines at the Sudz-N-Spin had front windows like aquariums, and Maika had learned to watch her clothes tumble the way other people watched television. Tonight her father's work shirts went around and around while she sat on the orange plastic bench with the driver's manual open on her knees, tracing the diagram of a car sliding into a parking space between two others. She had failed the road test once already. The examiner had written something about her parallel parking, and something about merging, and she had not read the sheet twice because once had been visceral enough, a cold drop straight down the spine, and she preferred not to revisit it.

"Still studying?" Julien came in carrying a duffel of towels, because his building's machine had died a week ago and he refused to admit it. He dropped onto the bench beside her and peered at the diagram. "That looks easy. You just turn the wheel."

"If it were easy I would have passed," Maika said. She turned the page and found the section on following distance, which she had skipped before, confident, wrongly, that the test would never ask. The manual said to keep at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead, and a longer gap in rain, snow or darkness. She read it twice. "Two seconds," she said aloud. "How do you even count two seconds in a car?"

"You count, dummy. Like this." Julien held up a hand, watched a man carry a basket past the window, and began counting the moment the man crossed the doorframe. "One Mississippi, two Mississippi." The man's shoulder cleared the gum machine on the second one. "You pick something on the road, a sign or a pole, and when the car ahead passes it you start counting. If you get to the sign before you finish counting, you're too close."

Maika looked at him. She had known Julien since seventh grade and had never suspected him of knowing anything the manual knew. "Who taught you that?"

"My cousin. He drives a delivery van." Julien shrugged, as if to say the information had arrived by accident and he made no claims for it. "Did they fail you for tailgating?"

"No. They failed me for the parking and the merge." She closed the manual and looked out at the parking lot, which at this hour held only four cars, widely spaced under the buzzing sodium light, and an idea arrived with the force of something obvious that had been standing behind her the whole time. "Julien. The lot. Could we use your mom's car?"

It took some negotiation. Julien remonstrated on the grounds that his mother counted the miles on the odometer the way misers counted coins, and Maika argued that the lot was private and the car would travel perhaps forty feet, and eventually they struck a bargain: he would drive it around from the street, she would not scratch it, and in exchange for his silence she would carry his towels in and out for a month. A full amnesty, she called it, for any future offenses of his she might otherwise report, and he agreed before she could list what those offenses might be.

Mr. Chatterjee, who owned the building and ran the laundromat and lived above it, came down while they were arranging traffic cones. He kept a stack of faded orange cones behind the ice machine for reasons no one had ever established, and when Maika asked if she could borrow four, he studied her with his hands folded behind his back. "Parallel parking," he said. It was not a question. "My daughter practiced in this lot thirty years ago. She parked between the cones for a week. Now she drives in Toronto." He carried the cones out himself and set them down with the precision of a man arranging flowers, and then he stood near the door to watch.

The first attempts were ugly. Maika brought the car in at too shallow an angle and ended up a foot from the curb, then overcorrected and climbed it entirely, one wheel lipping up onto the concrete with a sound that made Julien grip the dashboard. She sat still after that, engine idling, and instead of trying again she found herself thinking about the two-second rule, about how it converted distance into time, into something you could count out loud. The parking was the same problem in a different shape. It was not about feet. It was about when. When to turn the wheel, when the rear cone appeared in the side mirror at a certain angle, when to straighten. She stopped measuring with her eyes and started measuring with a sequence.

By the tenth attempt she could do it, slowly, with three or four corrections. By the fifteenth she could do it in two. Mr. Chatterjee, from the doorway, called out, "You are still looking at the cones. Look where you want the car to go." She tried it, keeping her eyes moving to the space itself rather than the obstacles around it, and the car slid in as if it had been waiting all evening for her to stop staring at what she feared. She sat in the parked car with her hands still on the wheel and felt something loosen in her chest.

The merge was harder, because the highway would not come to the laundromat. Julien drove them out to the ring road after the towels were dry, past eleven, and the dark complicated everything. Maika remembered the manual as the first drops began to hit the windshield, thin and greasy under the streetlights. Rain, and darkness too, so she counted to three and then to four behind the car ahead, watching a streetlamp pass the other car's trunk before the word three was fully out of her mouth, and adjusted. She liked the counting. It gave her something to do with her fear besides feel it. Julien, in the passenger seat, counted quietly along with her, and once, when she closed to two seconds without noticing, he said "gap," one syllable, and she fell back without being told twice.

On the ramp to the highway her mouth went dry and the fear was entirely visceral again, beyond counting, and she merged too slowly the first time, forcing the car behind to brake, its lights flaring in the mirror. The second ramp went better. The third, she found the gap, counted her way to it, and the car behind her never touched its brakes at all. She stayed in the right lane at a careful distance and did not try for more.

They came back to the dark laundromat lot at midnight. Mr. Chatterjee's window above was lit. Maika parked between two of the cones in one motion, killed the engine, and sat listening to the tick of the cooling motor. Julien gathered his towels. "So when's the retest?" he asked through the open window.

"Tuesday," she said. "But I'm coming back here Monday." She looked at the cones, small and orange and patient in the dark, and put her hand back on the key.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, which falls on April 4, 5 or 6, families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep and clean them and leave offerings of food.
story:
The temple smelled of sandalwood and oranges, an odd sweetness that Gabriella could not decide was comforting or too much. Her grandmother's photograph stood on the altar beneath a strip of red paper with characters Gabriella could not read, and around it, mourners she mostly did not know pressed their palms together and bowed. Her father had grown up in this building. Her mother had grown up in a church two suburbs over, and she stood near the back now with her coat buttoned to the throat, holding the hymnal someone had mistaken her for wanting.

The funeral itself was quiet, full of forms Gabriella could follow but not parse. Monks chanted. Incense smoke rose in a thin gray thread and bent when someone opened the side door. Gabriella copied her father's bow at the right moments, and when a woman with kind, crinkled eyes offered her a plate of rice, she took a small portion because refusing seemed worse than uncertainty.

Afterward, in the courtyard where paper ash drifted, her cousin found her. He was twenty-three, on her father's side, the one who had organized the altar flowers down to the chrysanthemums. "You'll come in spring," he said. It was not quite a question.

"Come where?"

"To the grave. Qingming. It falls on April 4th, 5th or 6th, depending on the year." He wiped his hands on his trousers as if he had already begun the work of it. "We go every year. We sweep the graves and clean them, and we leave food. Fruit, her sesame cakes if you can find them. It's what families do." He glanced toward Gabriella's mother, still in the doorway. "Your dad used to come. Before he married, he came every year."

Gabriella had heard the word Qingming exactly once, in her grandmother's kitchen, when the old woman was explaining something about her own mother's grave and Gabriella had been thirteen and hungry and not listening. That not-listening pressed on her now like a stone under the ribs. She watched her mother, who was talking to Ms. Fraser, the neighbor who had driven them here because Gabriella's father could not. Ms. Fraser kept touching her mother's arm. Her mother kept smiling in the way that meant she was holding herself together with visible effort.

The disagreement, when it came, was not loud. In the car, her mother said quietly that she was glad Dad had his rituals, that she believed the dead were with God and did not need sesame cakes left in the rain. She said it without cruelty, which somehow made it harder to answer. Gabriella knew her mother's faith had carried her through her own mother's funeral eight years ago, an asceticism of sorts, plain hymns and plain bread, nothing wasted on ornament. And she knew her father had not swept a grave in nineteen years, and that today, in the courtyard, he had looked like a man reminded of a debt.

That night Gabriella could not sleep, so she called Rhianna, who was good at sitting with a problem instead of solving it. "You don't have to pick," Rhianna said, mid-yawn. "You're allowed to do both badly." Gabriella laughed for the first time in four days. It had catalyzed something, that permission, small as a match struck in a dark room. She wrote in her notebook, the one for college lists and scholarship deadlines, two columns: prayer, and sweeping. She looked at them for a long time. She did not draw a line between them, and she did not cross either out.

In April, on the 5th, she took the bus to the cemetery with her cousin and her father. Her mother had kissed her at the door and said, "Say something to her for me," which Gabriella understood to be its own kind of crossing over. The morning was cold for spring, the grass wet, and her grandmother's stone had a thin pelt of winter grime along its base. Her cousin handed her a stiff brush. Together they swept, small strokes, the sound like whispering, and then he set out the oranges and the sesame cakes on a cloth, arranging them as carefully as he had arranged the chrysanthemums.

Gabriella knelt in the wet grass and pressed her palms together, the way the mourners had done in the temple, and then, because her mother was also her mother, she bowed her head and said the words she knew from the plain church. Whether her grandmother heard anything at all, in any direction, through any door, Gabriella could not say, and she found she could live with not saying. She placed the third orange a little apart from the others, where her mother's hello could sit, and stayed kneeling while the steam of her breath faded over the stone.

"Some for her and some for us," her cousin said, breaking a sesame cake in half and holding the warm piece out to her.
